q: What is the difference between AI, machine learning, deep learning and data science?

AI is the broad goal of making machines do things that need intelligence. Machine learning is the part of AI where the system learns patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks and shines on images, audio and text. Data science is the wider job: collecting and cleaning data, analysing it, building models if they help, and turning the result into a decision. A data scientist uses machine learning as one tool among several.
Also covers: general vs applied AI, statistics vs ML.

A bank asks why customers leave. The data scientist cleans the data, charts it and runs tests (data science), trains a model to score churn risk (machine learning), and for call recordings uses a neural network (deep learning), all inside the bank's wider AI strategy.
What are supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, self-supervised and reinforcement learning?

Supervised learning learns from examples that come with the right answer (labels), for tasks like predicting a price or a class. Unsupervised learning has no labels and looks for structure, such as clusters or unusual points. Semi-supervised mixes a small labelled set with a large unlabelled one. Self-supervised creates its own labels from the data, for example hiding a word and predicting it, which is how large language models are pre-trained. Reinforcement learning has an agent act, receive rewards, and learn a strategy that maximises them over time.
Also covers: regression vs classification, common unsupervised tasks (clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, association rules).

Predicting house prices from past sales is supervised. Grouping shoppers by behaviour with no preset groups is unsupervised. A robot learning to walk over unknown ground by trial and reward is reinforcement learning.
Walk me through the end-to-end lifecycle of a machine learning project.

I start with the business problem and how success will be measured, then check the data exists and is allowed to be used. Next come data collection, cleaning and exploration, then splitting into train, validation and test sets before any decisions are made from the data. I build a simple baseline first, then engineer features, train and compare models, and tune with cross-validation. I judge the final model once on the untouched test set, deploy it behind an API or batch job, monitor drift and accuracy, and retrain when it degrades. It is a loop, not a line.
Also covers: business understanding, EDA, baseline, deployment, monitoring.

A telecom wants fewer cancellations. The team defines success as 'catch 60% of churners at under 20% false alarms', builds a logistic-regression baseline, beats it with gradient boosting, ships a weekly score to the retention team, and retrains when the score quality drops.
What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter?

Parameters are the numbers the model learns from data during training, such as the coefficients in a regression or the weights in a neural network. Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training that control how learning happens, such as tree depth, learning rate or the number of neighbours. You do not learn hyperparameters by fitting the training data directly; you try values and compare results on validation data.
In a random forest, each tree's split thresholds are parameters learned from data. The number of trees and the maximum depth are hyperparameters you pick and tune.
Why do we split data into training, validation and test sets?

Training data teaches the model. Validation data is used to compare models and tune settings. Test data is kept locked away and used once at the end to estimate how the model will do on genuinely new data. If you tune against the test set, you quietly fit to it and your final score becomes too optimistic. With small data, cross-validation replaces a fixed validation set.
Also covers: what 'labelled data' means, why we hold data out.

You have 10,000 rows. You use 7,000 to train, 1,500 to choose between three models, and 1,500 once to report the final score. If the final score is much worse than validation, you were overfitting your choices.
Explain the bias-variance trade-off.

Prediction error comes from three places: bias, variance and noise you cannot remove. Bias is error from a model being too simple to capture the real pattern, so it is wrong in the same way every time (underfitting). Variance is error from a model being so flexible that it changes a lot when the training data changes, so it chases noise (overfitting). Making a model more complex lowers bias but raises variance. The goal is the sweet spot where total error on new data is smallest. Regularization, more data and ensembles help move along this curve.
Also covers: irreducible error, bulls-eye diagram, why bagging cuts variance and boosting cuts bias.

Fitting a straight line to a curved trend is high bias: it misses the curve however much data you add. Fitting a 20th-degree polynomial through 25 points is high variance: it wiggles through every noisy point and fails on the next sample.
What are overfitting and underfitting, and how do you detect and fix them?

Overfitting means the model has memorised noise in the training data, so training scores are high and new-data scores are much lower. Underfitting means the model is too simple, so scores are poor on both. I detect them by comparing training and validation scores and by looking at learning curves. To fix overfitting: more data, simpler model, regularization, dropout, early stopping, fewer or better features. To fix underfitting: a richer model, better features, less regularization, longer training.
Also covers: learning curves, early stopping.

A tree grown with no depth limit scores 100% on training and 72% on validation (overfitting). Limiting depth to 6 gives 85% and 83%, a healthier gap. A depth-1 stump scoring 65% on both is underfitting.
What is cross-validation and what are its variants?

Cross-validation splits the data into k folds, trains on k-1 of them, tests on the remaining one, and repeats so every fold is the test fold once. The average score is a steadier estimate than one split, and the spread shows how stable the model is. Stratified k-fold keeps class proportions in every fold, which matters for imbalanced data. Group k-fold keeps all rows of one person or customer together to avoid leakage. For time series you must use forward-chaining splits so the model never trains on the future.
Also covers: stratified CV, group CV, leave-one-out, time-series CV.
With 5% fraud cases, a plain random split could put almost no fraud in a validation fold. Stratified 5-fold keeps about 5% in every fold, so each score is meaningful.
What is the curse of dimensionality?

As the number of features grows, the space they live in grows exponentially, so the same amount of data becomes very sparse. Points become far apart and distances between them look more and more alike, which hurts methods that depend on distance such as k-nearest neighbours and clustering, and makes it easy for any model to find chance patterns. The remedies are more data, fewer features (selection), dimensionality reduction such as PCA, regularization, or models that cope better with many features.
Also covers: p much larger than n, feature selection as a remedy.

A dataset with 100 rows and 100 features lets a model find 'rules' that are pure coincidence. Cutting to the 10 features that matter, or using L1 regularization, makes the findings far more trustworthy.
What is data leakage and how do you prevent it?

Data leakage is when information that would not be available at prediction time gets into training, so results look excellent in testing and then collapse in production. Typical causes: a feature that is a consequence of the target, scaling or imputing on the whole dataset before splitting, duplicates across train and test, and random splits on time-ordered data. I prevent it by splitting first, fitting every preprocessing step on training data only (using a pipeline), thinking about when each feature becomes known, and using time-based or group-based splits where needed.
Also covers: target leakage, train-test contamination, pipelines.
A model predicts loan default using 'collections call made'. That only happens after a default, so accuracy looks like 97% in testing. Drop the column and the real accuracy of 80% appears.
What is the difference between parametric and non-parametric methods, and between prediction and inference?

A parametric model assumes a fixed shape with a set number of parameters, like linear regression, so it is simple, fast and easy to interpret but can be wrong if the assumption is wrong. A non-parametric model, like k-nearest neighbours or a tree, lets the shape grow with the data, so it is flexible but needs more data and can overfit. Prediction cares only about getting accurate outputs, so flexible black boxes are fine. Inference cares about understanding how inputs affect the output, so simple, interpretable models are preferred.
Also covers: flexibility vs interpretability.
To forecast tomorrow's sales you may use a boosted tree (prediction). To tell the board how much a 10% discount changes sales you would use a regression with interpretable coefficients (inference).
What is the difference between interpolation and extrapolation?

Interpolation estimates a value inside the range of data you have seen; extrapolation estimates it outside that range. Interpolation is usually reliable, while extrapolation is risky because the pattern may not continue and many models, especially trees, cannot predict beyond the values they trained on. A time-series forecast is extrapolation by nature, which is why it needs careful validation.
A model trained on house sizes from 40 to 200 square metres predicts a 120 sq m house well (interpolation). Asking it about a 900 sq m mansion is extrapolation and the answer is a guess.
What are online learning and out-of-core learning?

Online learning updates the model as data arrives, a piece at a time, instead of retraining on everything. It suits data that streams in or patterns that keep changing. Out-of-core learning is for data too big to fit in memory: you read it in chunks and update the model chunk by chunk. They are often combined. Beware of forgetting old patterns and of bad data quickly corrupting the model.
Also covers: partial_fit in scikit-learn, concept drift.
A spam filter that learns from every 'report spam' click, updating a little each hour, is online learning. Training a linear model on 500 GB of logs by reading 1 GB at a time is out-of-core.
How do you choose which algorithm to use for a problem?

I begin with the question: what is the target, how much data is there, do I need to explain the result, and what are the latency and cost limits? For tabular data I start with a regularised linear or logistic model as a baseline, then try gradient-boosted trees, which are often the strongest. For images, audio and text I use neural networks, usually starting from a pre-trained model. For few rows, simple models; for very many rows, more flexible ones. I compare on the same cross-validation split, and the winner is the simplest model that meets the need.
Also covers: baseline-first, no free lunch.

For a 20,000-row customer table, logistic regression gets AUC 0.78, a random forest 0.83 and gradient boosting 0.85. If the business needs explanations, you might pick the boosted model plus SHAP, or accept 0.83 with a simpler story.
What is linear regression and what assumptions does it make?

Linear regression fits a straight line (or a plane in many dimensions) that predicts a number from inputs by minimising the sum of squared errors. For the coefficients and their p-values to be trustworthy it assumes: a roughly linear relationship, independent errors, constant error variance (homoscedasticity), errors that are roughly normal (mainly for small samples and intervals), and no severe multicollinearity. For pure prediction, the model can still work when some assumptions are bent.
Also covers: Y = mX + c, least squares, residual plots.
Predicting salary from years of experience: salary = 30,000 + 4,000 x years. A plot of residuals that fans out as experience grows shows the constant-variance assumption is broken.
How do you read an OLS summary (coefficients, t-values, p-values, R-squared, F-statistic)?

Each coefficient says how much the target changes for a one-unit change in that feature, holding the others fixed. The t-value is the coefficient divided by its standard error; a large absolute t, equivalently a small p-value, says the effect is unlikely to be zero by chance. The confidence interval gives a plausible range for the coefficient. R-squared shows the share of variance explained, and the F-statistic tests whether the model as a whole beats a model with no features. In Python, statsmodels prints all of this with model.summary().
Also covers: null hypothesis for a coefficient, confidence intervals.
If the coefficient for 'ad spend' is 2.1 with p = 0.003 and interval [0.9, 3.3], each extra unit of spend is associated with about 2.1 more sales, and zero effect is unlikely.
What is R-squared and adjusted R-squared, and can R-squared be negative?

R-squared is the share of the target's variation that the model explains, 1 minus the model's squared error divided by the squared error of just predicting the mean. On the training data of an ordinary least-squares model with an intercept it lies between 0 and 1, and it never goes down when you add a feature, even a useless one. Adjusted R-squared penalises extra features, so it only rises if a new feature helps more than chance would. On new data R-squared can be negative, which means the model is worse than predicting the average.
Also covers: why R-squared alone can mislead.
Adding a column of random numbers nudges R-squared from 0.700 to 0.702, but adjusted R-squared falls from 0.690 to 0.688, correctly saying the column is useless.
What are MSE, RMSE and MAE, and how do you choose?

MSE is the average squared error; RMSE is its square root, in the same units as the target; MAE is the average absolute error. Squaring makes large errors count much more, so MSE and RMSE are sensitive to outliers and are right when big misses are especially costly. MAE treats every unit of error equally and is more robust and easy to explain. Huber loss is a compromise. The training loss and the reporting metric can differ, so choose the metric that matches business cost.
Also covers: Huber loss, MAPE.
Two forecasts miss by 1, 1, 1, 1 and 0, 0, 0, 4. Both have MAE 1, but the second has RMSE 2, so RMSE flags that it occasionally misses badly.
What are L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) regularization, and what is elastic net?

Both add a penalty on large coefficients to the loss so the model cannot fit noise so freely. Ridge (L2) penalises the sum of squared coefficients: it shrinks all coefficients smoothly but rarely to exactly zero, and handles correlated features well. Lasso (L1) penalises the sum of absolute values: it can push some coefficients exactly to zero, so it does feature selection. Elastic net blends both, which helps when features are correlated and you also want sparsity. The penalty strength, usually called lambda or alpha, is a hyperparameter chosen by cross-validation, and features should be scaled first.
Also covers: sparse solutions, lambda = 0 equals OLS, very large lambda underfits.

With 200 candidate features and 500 rows, lasso keeps 18 features with non-zero coefficients, giving a model you can explain, while ridge keeps all 200 with small weights and may predict slightly better.
Why does L1 produce zeros while L2 does not?

Think of the constraint region the coefficients must stay inside. For L1 it is a diamond with sharp corners on the axes; for L2 it is a smooth circle. The error contours usually touch the diamond at a corner, where some coefficients are exactly zero, while they touch the circle at a point where none are. In gradient terms, the L1 penalty pushes with a constant force toward zero no matter how small the coefficient, but the L2 push shrinks as the coefficient shrinks.
Imagine two equally useful, nearly identical features. Ridge gives both a half share; lasso tends to keep one and drop the other, which is why lasso can be unstable on highly correlated features.
What is heteroscedasticity and how do you handle it?

Heteroscedasticity means the spread of the errors changes across the range of the predictions, for example small errors for cheap items and huge errors for expensive ones. Ordinary least squares still gives unbiased coefficients, but its standard errors and p-values become unreliable. I spot it with a residuals-versus-fitted plot or tests such as Breusch-Pagan. Fixes: transform the target (log), use per-capita or rate variables, weighted least squares, robust standard errors, or add a missing variable that explains the changing spread.
Also covers: pure vs impure heteroscedasticity, weighted regression.
Predicting company revenue, errors for small firms are in the thousands and for big firms in the millions. Modelling log(revenue) usually makes the spread roughly constant.
What is multicollinearity and how do you detect and treat it?

Multicollinearity means two or more features are strongly correlated, so the model cannot separate their individual effects. Coefficients become unstable, with large standard errors and flipping signs, even though overall predictions may stay accurate. I detect it with a correlation matrix and the variance inflation factor, VIF = 1 / (1 - R-squared of that feature regressed on the others), where values above about 5 to 10 are a warning. I treat it by dropping or combining features, using PCA, ridge regression, or centering before creating interaction terms. If you only need predictions, it is often harmless.
Also covers: VIF, dummy variable trap.
'Height in cm' and 'height in inches' both in a model: coefficients become huge opposite numbers that cancel out. Dropping one fixes it with no loss of accuracy.
What is logistic regression and how does it work?

Logistic regression predicts the probability of a class, usually yes or no. It computes a weighted sum of features (just like linear regression) and passes it through the sigmoid function, which squeezes any number into a value between 0 and 1. You then pick a threshold, often 0.5, to turn the probability into a class. It is trained by maximising the likelihood, equivalent to minimising log loss (cross-entropy), not squared error. Its coefficients are easy to explain, which is why it remains a strong baseline.
Also covers: sigmoid, log-odds, cost function, threshold.
A bank's model gives a loan applicant a score of z = 1.2; the sigmoid turns that into a 77% probability of repayment. With a 0.5 threshold the loan is approved.
Why can't we use linear regression for a classification problem?

Linear regression output is unbounded, so it can predict -3 or 1.7 where a probability must stay between 0 and 1. It is also pulled around by extreme points, so a single very large tumour could shift the line and move the decision boundary, and squared error is not the right loss for categories. Logistic regression fixes both by modelling the probability through the sigmoid and training with log loss.
Fit a line to tumour size (0 = benign, 1 = malignant). Add one huge malignant tumour and the 0.5 cut-off shifts, so some previously correct cases flip, which a probability model would not do.
How do you interpret the coefficients of a logistic regression?

Each coefficient is the change in the log-odds of the outcome for a one-unit rise in that feature, holding others fixed. Raising e to that power gives the odds ratio, which is easier to say: a coefficient of 0.69 means the odds roughly double. The effect on probability itself is not constant; it depends on where you start. Scale or standardise features if you want to compare their importance.
Also covers: odds vs probability, odds ratio.
If 'late payments last year' has coefficient 0.4, the odds ratio is e^0.4 which is about 1.5, so each extra late payment multiplies the odds of default by about 1.5.
How does logistic regression handle more than two classes?

There are two common ways. One-vs-rest trains one yes/no model per class and picks the class with the highest score. Multinomial (softmax) regression learns all classes together and uses the softmax function to turn the scores into probabilities that add up to 1. Softmax is usually preferred when classes are mutually exclusive. The loss is categorical cross-entropy.
Also covers: softmax, multinomial.
Classifying a support ticket as billing, technical or sales: the model scores 2.0, 0.5 and -1.0 and softmax converts them into 78%, 17% and 4%.
What is polynomial regression, and what are generalised linear models?

Polynomial regression adds powers of a feature (x, x squared, x cubed) to a linear model so it can fit curves; it is still linear in the coefficients. High degrees overfit and behave wildly at the edges. Generalised linear models extend linear regression to targets that are not normally distributed by using a link function: logistic regression for yes/no, Poisson regression for counts, and gamma regression for positive skewed amounts.
Predicting the number of daily support calls (a count) with Poisson regression keeps predictions positive, while ordinary regression could predict -2 calls.
What is support vector regression (SVR) and how is it different from ordinary regression?

Ordinary regression tries to make every error small. SVR ignores errors that fall inside a tube of width epsilon around the prediction and only penalises points outside the tube, so the points on or outside the tube become the support vectors that define the fit. A parameter C sets how hard to punish those outside points, and kernels such as RBF allow curved fits. It works well on medium-sized data but scales poorly to very large sets, and needs scaled features.
Also covers: epsilon-insensitive loss, kernel, support vectors.
Predicting delivery time, you decide an error under 5 minutes does not matter. SVR with epsilon = 5 spends its effort on the orders that are off by more than 5 minutes.
How do you check whether a regression model is trustworthy?

I look at residuals: plotted against predictions they should show no pattern and constant spread; a QQ plot checks rough normality; a time or order plot checks independence. I check for influential points with leverage and Cook's distance, check VIF for collinearity, and validate on held-out data with RMSE or MAE rather than trusting in-sample R-squared. I also look at the biggest errors to understand where the model fails.
Also covers: QQ plot, Cook's distance, Durbin-Watson.
A residual plot shaped like a U means the straight-line assumption is wrong; adding a squared term or switching to a tree model typically fixes it.
Gradient descent or the normal equation: how can linear regression be solved?

Linear regression has a closed-form answer called the normal equation, which solves for the coefficients directly but needs matrix inversion, so it becomes slow and numerically fragile with very many features. Gradient descent starts anywhere and repeatedly steps downhill on the loss, scales to huge data (especially in mini-batches), and also works for models with no closed form, such as neural networks. For small and medium problems libraries use stable matrix methods; for huge ones, stochastic gradient descent.
Also covers: learning rate, convergence, feature scaling for gradient descent.
With 50 features and 10,000 rows, a solver finds the answer instantly. With 10 million rows and 500,000 sparse features, mini-batch gradient descent is the practical choice.
What is a decision tree and how does it make predictions?

A decision tree asks a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as 'is income above 50,000?', splitting the data into purer and purer groups until it reaches leaves. A new example follows the questions down to a leaf and gets that leaf's majority class (or average value for regression). Trees need no scaling, handle numbers and categories, capture non-linear patterns and are easy to explain, but a single deep tree overfits badly.
Also covers: nodes and leaves, classification vs regression trees.
A loan tree might say: income above 50k? yes. Existing debt below 10k? yes. Approve. Every decision is a path you can read out loud to a customer.
What are entropy, information gain and Gini impurity?

They measure how mixed a node is, so the tree can choose the split that makes children purer. Entropy is minus the sum of p times log2(p) over classes: 0 for a pure node and, for two classes, 1 at a 50/50 mix. Information gain is the parent's entropy minus the weighted average entropy of the children; pick the split with the biggest gain. Gini impurity is 1 minus the sum of p squared: 0 when pure, 0.5 at a 50/50 mix for two classes; pick the split with the lowest weighted Gini. They usually produce very similar trees, and Gini is slightly cheaper to compute.
Also covers: ID3, C4.5, CART. Note: some study notes call the sum of p squared 'Gini' and pick the highest; the standard impurity is 1 minus that and you pick the lowest.
A node with 10 positives and 10 negatives has Gini 0.5. A split into (9 positive, 1 negative) and (1 positive, 9 negative) gives each child Gini 0.18, a large improvement, so that split wins.
How do you control tree growth and what is pruning?

An unrestricted tree keeps splitting until it memorises the training data. Pre-pruning (early stopping) limits growth with settings such as maximum depth, minimum samples to split and minimum samples per leaf. Post-pruning grows a full tree and then cuts back branches that do not improve validation performance, for example using cost-complexity pruning, where a penalty (alpha, or CP in R) trades tree size against error. In practice I tune these with cross-validation.
Also covers: max_depth, min_samples_leaf, ccp_alpha.
A tree with 400 leaves scores 100% train and 78% validation. Setting min_samples_leaf = 30 shrinks it to 25 leaves and lifts validation to 84%.
How do trees handle numerical, categorical and missing values?

For a numeric feature the tree tries thresholds and picks the best cut ('age <= 37'). For a category it groups categories into two sets, or, in many libraries, you must encode categories to numbers first. Implementations differ on missing values: some learn a default direction for missing values (XGBoost, LightGBM, histogram gradient boosting in scikit-learn), while others require imputation. Trees do not need scaling because they only compare values within a feature.
Also covers: label vs one-hot encoding for trees.
Giving a tree a 'city' column encoded 0 to 49 can make it treat cities as ordered. For a plain tree, one-hot or a library with native categorical support avoids that.
What is a random forest and why does it work?

A random forest trains many decision trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the rows and, at every split, considering only a random subset of the features. Because the trees are different and make partly independent mistakes, averaging their votes (or predictions) cancels much of the noise, cutting variance without raising bias much. It needs little tuning, handles mixed data, gives feature importances and an out-of-bag error estimate, but it is larger and slower to predict than one tree.
Also covers: bagging, max_features, n_estimators, n_jobs, out-of-bag score.
One tree says 'default' for a customer; 300 trees trained on different samples vote 220 to 80 for 'no default'. The majority is more reliable than any single tree.
How do you measure feature importance in tree models, and what are the pitfalls?

Impurity-based importance (feature_importances_) sums how much each feature reduced impurity across splits; it is fast but biased toward features with many distinct values and can mislead with correlated features. Permutation importance shuffles one feature on held-out data and measures how much the score drops, which is more honest. SHAP values give per-prediction contributions that add up to the prediction. Importance describes what the model uses, not causal effect.
Also covers: SHAP, permutation importance.
A random ID column can rank high on impurity importance in a tree model because it has unique values, but permutation importance on test data correctly gives it zero.
What is the difference between bagging and boosting?

Both combine many weak models. Bagging trains models independently on random resamples of the data and averages them, which mainly reduces variance; random forest is the classic example. Boosting trains models one after another, each one focusing on the mistakes of the previous ones, which mainly reduces bias and often gives higher accuracy, but it is more sensitive to noisy labels and needs more careful tuning. Bagging is easy to run in parallel; boosting is sequential.
Also covers: weak learner, ensemble, bootstrap.
Ten friends each guess the weight of a cow independently and you average (bagging). Alternatively, each friend sees the previous friends' errors and corrects them (boosting).
How does AdaBoost work?

AdaBoost starts by giving every training example the same weight and fits a very simple model, often a one-split tree called a stump. It then raises the weights of examples that were misclassified and lowers the rest, so the next stump concentrates on the hard cases. Each stump gets a say in the final vote according to its accuracy. It was the first practical boosting method; it is sensitive to outliers and label noise.
If the first stump wrongly labels 20 of 100 emails, those 20 become more important, and the second stump tries especially hard to get them right.
How does gradient boosting work?

Gradient boosting builds trees one at a time, where each new tree is trained to predict the errors (more exactly, the negative gradient of the loss) of the current ensemble. You add its output scaled by a small learning rate, so many small corrections add up to a strong model. Key hyperparameters are the number of trees, learning rate, tree depth, subsampling and regularization; early stopping on a validation set decides when to stop. It tends to be the best performer on structured, tabular data.
Also covers: residuals, learning rate, shrinkage, early stopping.
To predict house prices, tree 1 predicts 300k for a house worth 350k. Tree 2 is trained to predict the +50k miss, tree 3 the remaining miss, and so on until the errors are small.
What are the differences between XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost?

All three are fast, regularised gradient-boosting libraries. XGBoost popularised the approach with careful regularization, missing-value handling and strong engineering. LightGBM is built for speed on large data using histogram binning and grows trees leaf-wise, which is fast and accurate but can overfit small data without limits. CatBoost handles categorical features natively with a technique that avoids target leakage and is often strong with little tuning. Details change between versions, so check current documentation.
Also covers: histogram-based splits, categorical handling, GPU support.
On a table with many high-cardinality columns such as city and product, CatBoost may do well with defaults, while for 50 million rows LightGBM may train fastest.
Why do gradient-boosted trees often beat deep learning on tabular data?

Tabular data has mixed types, uneven feature importance, few rows relative to images or text, and no spatial or sequential structure for a neural network to exploit. Trees handle irregular, non-smooth relationships, need no scaling, cope with missing values and train quickly on modest data. Neural networks can match them with a lot of data and careful tuning, and they win when you need embeddings, multi-modal inputs or end-to-end learning, but boosting is the strong default.
On a 100,000-row customer table, a boosted model can reach its best score in minutes on a laptop, while a neural network needs tuning of architecture, scaling and embeddings to get close.
What are stacking, blending and voting ensembles?

Voting averages (or takes the majority of) several different models. Stacking trains a second-level model on the predictions of the first-level models, learned from out-of-fold predictions so it does not see leaked labels. Blending is a simpler version that trains the second level on a held-out slice. They help most when the base models are diverse and individually decent, at the cost of complexity and slower serving.
Combining a logistic regression, a random forest and a boosted model by letting a small logistic regression weigh their predictions often adds a little accuracy over the best single model.
What is out-of-bag (OOB) error?

Each bootstrap sample used by a tree leaves out roughly a third of the rows. For each row, you average only the trees that did not see it, giving a prediction that works like a validation prediction. The OOB score is therefore a free estimate of test performance without a separate validation set. It is useful for quick checks, but cross-validation is still better for fine model comparison.
Training a random forest on 5,000 customers, the OOB accuracy of 86% lets you see how it will do before you set anything aside.
Which hyperparameters matter most in gradient boosting, and what is early stopping?

The ones I tune first are the learning rate with the number of trees (lower rate, more trees), tree depth or number of leaves, minimum samples or weight per leaf, subsampling of rows and columns, and L1/L2 regularization. Early stopping watches the validation score after each added tree and stops when it has not improved for a set number of rounds, so you do not have to guess the number of trees.
Setting learning rate 0.05 with up to 2,000 trees and early stopping after 50 rounds might stop at tree 640 where validation loss was lowest.
What is a support vector machine (SVM)?

An SVM finds the dividing line (hyperplane) between two classes that leaves the widest possible margin to the nearest points on either side; those nearest points are the support vectors, and only they matter for the boundary. A soft margin lets some points be misclassified, controlled by the parameter C. It works well when there are many features, even more than samples, and with kernels it can draw curved boundaries. It slows down on very large datasets and needs scaled features.
Also covers: maximum margin, hard vs soft margin, hyperplane.
Separating two groups of customers on a 2D chart, the SVM draws the middle of the widest empty street between them; only the customers touching the street edges decide where it goes.
What is the kernel trick, and how do C and gamma affect an RBF SVM?

Some data cannot be split by a straight line, but would be separable if lifted into a higher dimension. The kernel trick computes the similarity as if the data were in that space, without actually building the extra features. Common kernels are linear, polynomial and RBF (the usual default). C controls the penalty for misclassifying: high C fits training data tightly and risks overfitting; low C allows a wider, simpler margin. Gamma sets how far one point's influence reaches in an RBF kernel: high gamma gives wiggly, local boundaries; low gamma gives smooth ones. Tune both together by cross-validation.
Also covers: polynomial and RBF kernels, strengths and weaknesses of SVM.
Points arranged as a ring around a centre cannot be split by a line in 2D, but an RBF kernel separates them by effectively adding a 'distance from the centre' dimension.
What is Naive Bayes and why is it called naive?

Naive Bayes uses Bayes' theorem to compute the probability of each class given the features, P(class | features) proportional to P(class) times the product of P(feature | class). It is called naive because it assumes the features are independent given the class, which is rarely true. Even so it works surprisingly well for text, trains and predicts extremely fast, handles many features, and needs little data. Its probability estimates are often poorly calibrated.
Also covers: Bayes' theorem, Gaussian, multinomial and Bernoulli variants, Laplace smoothing.

A spam filter multiplies the probability of each word in spam versus non-spam emails. 'Free', 'winner' and 'click' together make the spam probability very high, even though it ignores that these words often appear together.
What are Gaussian, multinomial and Bernoulli Naive Bayes, and when do you use each?

They differ in how they model each feature. Gaussian assumes continuous features follow a normal distribution within each class, with a mean and standard deviation per class, so it suits numeric data. Multinomial models counts, such as word counts or TF-IDF, and is the standard for text. Bernoulli models yes/no features, such as whether a word appears. Add smoothing so a word never seen in a class does not zero out the whole probability.
For classifying iris flowers by petal and sepal measurements, use Gaussian. For classifying news articles by word counts, use multinomial.
Explain Bayes' theorem and why base rates matter.

Bayes' theorem updates a belief with evidence: P(A given B) = P(B given A) x P(A) / P(B). The prior P(A), the base rate, matters because ignoring it makes rare events look likely after a positive test. Even an accurate test can produce mostly false alarms when the thing being tested for is rare.
Also covers: prior, likelihood, posterior, base-rate fallacy.

A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people; a test is 99% sensitive with a 5% false-positive rate. Out of 1,000 people, about 1 true case tests positive and about 50 healthy people also do, so a positive result means only about a 2% chance of disease.
How does k-nearest neighbours (KNN) work and how do you choose k?

KNN stores the training data and, to predict for a new point, finds the k closest training points and takes a majority vote (classification) or an average (regression). It is called lazy because there is no training step; all the work happens at prediction time, which gets slow on large data. A small k gives a flexible, noisy boundary (low bias, high variance); a large k gives a smoother one (higher bias). I choose k with cross-validation, often an odd number for two classes to avoid ties.
Also covers: lazy learning, instance-based learning, bias-variance in k.
To classify a new song's genre, find the 5 most similar songs in your library; if 4 are jazz, predict jazz.
What distance metrics does KNN use, and why does scaling matter?

Euclidean distance is the default for continuous features, Manhattan distance suits high dimensions or grid-like data, cosine similarity is common for text and embeddings, and Hamming distance compares categorical or binary features. Because KNN is driven by distances, a feature measured in thousands drowns out one measured in single digits, so standardise or normalise features first. Distances also lose meaning in very high dimensions, so reduce dimensions first.
Also covers: KNN regression vs classification, curse of dimensionality.
With age (20 to 60) and income (20,000 to 200,000), income dominates every distance. After standardising, both features contribute fairly.
What is a Gaussian mixture model and the EM algorithm?

A Gaussian mixture model says the data comes from several overlapping bell-shaped clusters, each with its own mean and spread, and gives each point a soft probability of belonging to each cluster. The expectation-maximisation (EM) algorithm fits it by alternating two steps: the E-step estimates each point's probability of belonging to each cluster using current parameters, and the M-step updates the parameters using those probabilities. It repeats until it stabilises, and can get stuck in local optima, so it is run from several starts. EM works whenever there are hidden variables.
Also covers: soft vs hard clustering, latent variables.

Heights of people from a school with the gender not recorded form two overlapping bumps. EM guesses two groups, assigns probabilities, recomputes the means and spreads, and converges on the male and female distributions.
What are linear and quadratic discriminant analysis (LDA, QDA)?

Both are classifiers that model each class as a Gaussian distribution and classify by which class is most probable. LDA assumes all classes share the same covariance, which gives straight-line boundaries and works well with small data. QDA lets each class have its own covariance, giving curved boundaries but needing more data. LDA can also be used for supervised dimension reduction. Do not confuse it with Latent Dirichlet Allocation, the topic model.
For two classes of customers with similar spread, LDA draws a straight cut; if one class is tightly clustered and the other widely spread, QDA's curved boundary fits better.
What is a confusion matrix?

A confusion matrix counts how a classifier's predictions line up with the truth. For two classes it has four cells: true positives (predicted yes, was yes), false positives (predicted yes, was no), true negatives and false negatives (predicted no, was yes). It shows not only how often the model is wrong but which kind of mistake it makes, which is what every other classification metric is calculated from. In scikit-learn, use confusion_matrix or ConfusionMatrixDisplay.
Also covers: TP, FP, TN, FN, multi-class matrices.
A fraud model flags 100 transactions: 80 are real fraud (TP) and 20 are fine (FP). It misses 40 real frauds (FN) and correctly clears 9,860 (TN).
What is accuracy, and when does it mislead?

Accuracy is the share of all predictions that are correct, (TP + TN) divided by everything. It misleads when classes are imbalanced or when the two kinds of error have different costs. A model that always predicts 'not fraud' is 99.9% accurate if only 0.1% of transactions are fraud, yet catches nothing. For such cases use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC or a cost-based metric.
Also covers: misclassification (error) rate = 1 - accuracy.
With 990 healthy and 10 sick patients, a model that says 'healthy' for everyone gets 99% accuracy and a recall of 0%.
What are precision, recall and F1, and how do you remember the formulas?

Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of everything I flagged, how much was right? Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate) = TP / (TP + FN): of everything that was truly positive, how much did I find? The F1 score is their harmonic mean, 2PR / (P + R), which is dragged toward the lower of the two, so you cannot hide a bad recall behind a good precision. Raising the threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall. Choose by the cost of each mistake. (Some study notes write recall's denominator as TP + FP; that is wrong, it is TP + FN.)
Also covers: F-beta, macro vs micro averaging, harmonic mean.
A fraud model with 80 true positives, 20 false positives and 40 missed frauds has precision 80/100 = 0.80 and recall 80/120 = 0.67, so F1 is about 0.73.
What are TPR, TNR, FPR and FNR (sensitivity and specificity)?

True positive rate (sensitivity, recall) is TP over all actual positives. True negative rate (specificity) is TN over all actual negatives. False positive rate is FP over all actual negatives, equal to 1 minus specificity. False negative rate is FN over all actual positives, equal to 1 minus recall. Medical tests are usually described by sensitivity and specificity; the ROC curve plots TPR against FPR.
A screening test with 95% sensitivity misses 5% of sick people (FNR 5%); with 90% specificity it raises a false alarm for 10% of healthy people (FPR 10%).
What is the ROC curve and AUC, and how do you interpret them?

The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as you sweep the decision threshold from strict to lenient. The area under it (AUC) summarises ranking quality: it is the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, so 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect. AUC does not depend on the threshold or on calibration, but with heavy class imbalance it can look flattering, so check the precision-recall curve too.
Also covers: AUC as probability of correct ranking, gini = 2 AUC - 1.
A churn model with AUC 0.85 means that if you pick one customer who left and one who stayed, the model scores the leaver higher 85% of the time.
When should you use the precision-recall curve instead of ROC?

When the positive class is rare and you care about finding it. ROC uses the false positive rate, whose denominator is the huge number of negatives, so even thousands of false alarms barely move it. Precision uses the number of flagged items as the denominator, so it reacts directly to false alarms. Average precision (area under the PR curve) is the summary; unlike ROC-AUC, its random baseline equals the positive rate, not 0.5.
With 0.1% fraud, a model can have ROC-AUC 0.97 yet only 10% precision at useful recall. The PR curve shows that, ROC does not.
How do you choose a classification threshold?

A model gives a probability; the threshold turns it into a decision and 0.5 is only a default. I put numbers on the cost of a false positive and a false negative, scan thresholds on validation data, and choose the one that minimises expected cost or hits a business constraint, such as 'at least 90% recall' or 'review capacity of 200 cases a day'. Then I check it still behaves on the test set and after calibration.
Also covers: cost-sensitive learning, operating point.
If missing a fraud costs 500 and a false alarm costs 5 for a human review, the best threshold is far below 0.5; you would flag any transaction above about 1% fraud probability.
How do you handle imbalanced classes?

First try the true distribution with the right metric and threshold. Then options: class weights (cost-sensitive learning), which is usually the simplest; oversampling the minority (random duplication or SMOTE, which creates synthetic neighbours); undersampling the majority; and ensembles built for imbalance. Resample only the training folds, never the validation or test data, or you leak. Evaluate with precision, recall, PR-AUC, not accuracy. Mild imbalance is often fine with no resampling.
Also covers: up-sampling, down-sampling, SMOTE, class_weight, imbalanced-learn.
With 2% positives, setting class_weight='balanced' in logistic regression often lifts recall from 30% to 70% at some cost in precision, which you then trade off with the threshold.
What are log loss and calibration, and why do they matter?

Log loss (cross-entropy) measures the quality of predicted probabilities, punishing confident wrong answers very heavily. A model is calibrated when its predicted probabilities match reality: of everything scored 0.8, about 80% should be positive. This matters when you use the probability itself, for pricing, risk or ranking by expected value. Check with a reliability curve and the Brier score, and fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression, for example CalibratedClassifierCV in scikit-learn.
Also covers: Brier score, reliability diagram.
A model says 90% likely to repay but only 70% of such applicants do. Even if its ranking is good (high AUC), using 90% in pricing would underprice risk until you calibrate it.
Which metrics do you use for regression, ranking and forecasting?

Regression: MAE, RMSE, R-squared, and for relative error MAPE (careful near zero) or a symmetric version. Ranking and recommendation: precision at k, recall at k, mean average precision and NDCG, which rewards putting the best items at the top. Forecasting: MAE, RMSE, MAPE or sMAPE, and MASE, which compares to a naive forecast. Always compare against a naive baseline.
Also covers: MASE, NDCG, precision@k.
A recommender shows 10 items and the user clicks the 2nd. Precision@10 is 0.1, while NDCG rewards that the click was near the top.
Compare grid search, random search and Bayesian optimisation for hyperparameter tuning.

Grid search tries every combination in a grid; it is thorough but explodes with more settings. Random search samples combinations and often finds equally good values in far fewer runs because only a few hyperparameters usually matter. Bayesian optimisation builds a model of how scores depend on settings and chooses the next trial where improvement looks most likely, so it needs fewer runs for expensive models. Tools: GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV in scikit-learn; Optuna is a popular Bayesian-style library (verify its current API). Always tune with cross-validation and keep a final test set.
Also covers: BayesSearchCV (scikit-optimize), successive halving.
Tuning 5 hyperparameters with 5 values each is 3,125 grid runs. Random search with 60 samples often reaches a near-best score at under 2% of the cost.
What is a scikit-learn Pipeline and why use one?

A Pipeline chains preprocessing steps (imputing, scaling, encoding) and a model into one object with fit and predict. It guarantees the same steps are applied in training and prediction, and when you cross-validate the whole pipeline each fold fits the preprocessing only on its own training part, which prevents leakage. ColumnTransformer applies different steps to different columns. The pipeline can be passed to GridSearchCV and saved as one file.
Also covers: transformers vs estimators, ColumnTransformer, SimpleImputer (the old Imputer class was removed).
A pipeline fills missing ages with the median, one-hot encodes city, scales income and fits logistic regression. You save it with joblib and the web service calls pipeline.predict on raw data.
How do learning curves help you diagnose a model?

A learning curve plots training and validation scores as the training set grows. If both are low and close, the model is underfitting: add capacity or features. If training is high and validation is much lower, it is overfitting: get more data, regularise or simplify. If validation is still rising when data runs out, more data would help. It tells you where effort will pay off before you spend it.
Training accuracy of 98% and validation of 80% that has flattened means more of the same data will not fix it; reduce complexity or add informative features.
How do you compare models fairly, and when is a difference real?

Compare them on the same data splits, with the same preprocessing, using repeated cross-validation, and look at the spread, not only the average. A 0.3% gap with a standard deviation of 1% is noise. For classical statistical models, AIC and BIC compare fit penalised for complexity (lower is better). For two classifiers on one test set, a paired test such as McNemar's can help. Also weigh simplicity, speed and explainability.
Also covers: AIC, BIC, McNemar's test, repeated CV.
Model A scores 0.842 and model B 0.846 across five folds with spreads of 0.01. That difference is within noise, so choose the simpler one.
What is data wrangling and what does it involve?

Data wrangling is turning raw data into something you can analyse: acquiring it, checking it is valid, current and relevant, cleaning it (fixing types, duplicates, impossible values, missing values and outliers), joining sources, reshaping it and creating features. It usually takes the largest share of a project, and errors here silently ruin everything after. I keep the steps in code so they are repeatable, and log how many rows each step removed.
Also covers: data cleaning, data validation, ETL.
Merging a customers table with an orders table, you find 3% duplicate customers, dates stored as text, and ages of 250. You dedupe, parse dates, cap impossible ages as missing, and record each fix.
How do you treat missing values?

First find out why they are missing: completely at random, related to other columns, or related to the missing value itself (for example, high earners skipping the income field), because that decides what is safe. If a column is mostly empty or useless, drop it; if only a few rows are affected, dropping may be fine. Otherwise impute: median or mean for numbers, most frequent or a 'missing' category for categories, or model-based imputation (KNN, iterative). Add a 'was missing' flag when missingness carries signal, and fit imputers on training data only. Tree-based boosting libraries can handle missing values natively.
Also covers: MCAR, MAR, MNAR, imputation, missing indicator.
In a loan table, 12% of income values are missing. Filling with the median and adding 'income_missing' lets the model learn that applicants who skip income are riskier.
How do you detect and handle outliers?

I look at the data first: box plots, histograms and scatter plots. Rules of thumb: a value more than about 3 standard deviations from the mean (works only if roughly normal), or outside 1.5 times the interquartile range beyond the quartiles (the box-plot rule). Then decide why it is there: a data error (fix or remove), a real rare event (keep, and maybe model separately), or a genuine extreme the model must handle (use robust methods or transform). Do not delete points just to improve a score.
Also covers: z-score, IQR, winsorising, robust models, isolation forest.
A salary column has one value of 9,000,000 among values around 60,000, which is a typo for 90,000. You correct it. A genuine CEO salary stays, and you use a log transform so it does not dominate.
What encoding techniques are there for categorical variables?

Label (ordinal) encoding maps categories to integers, fine for naturally ordered values like small, medium, large, and acceptable for trees, but it invents an order for unordered categories. One-hot encoding makes a 0/1 column per category, safe for linear and distance-based models but wide for high-cardinality features, and you drop one column to avoid the dummy-variable trap in linear models. For many categories use target (mean) encoding computed out-of-fold to avoid leakage, frequency encoding, hashing, or learned embeddings. Some libraries, like CatBoost, handle categories natively.
Also covers: dummy variable trap, target encoding, hashing, embeddings.
A 'city' column with 5,000 values would explode into 5,000 one-hot columns. Target encoding replaces each city with its average churn rate computed on training folds only.
What is the difference between normalization and standardization, and which models need scaling?

Normalization (min-max scaling) rescales a feature to a fixed range, usually 0 to 1: (x - min) / (max - min). Standardization (z-score) subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, giving mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Min-max is sensitive to outliers; standardization is the common default, and robust scaling uses median and IQR. Scaling matters for distance-based methods (KNN, k-means, SVM), gradient-descent models (linear and logistic regression, neural networks) and PCA. Tree-based models do not need it. Fit the scaler on training data only.
Also covers: StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler.
Phone prices (200 to 1,000) and storage (16 to 128): min-max turns both into 0 to 1 so neither dominates a distance calculation. A random forest would give the same result without scaling.
What is the difference between feature selection and feature extraction?

Feature selection keeps a subset of the original features and drops the rest, so the model stays interpretable. Methods: filter (statistics such as correlation or mutual information), wrapper (searching subsets with the model, like recursive feature elimination) and embedded (the model selects while training, like lasso or tree importances). Feature extraction creates new features from the old ones, such as PCA components, autoencoder codes, or n-grams from text, which can compress information but are harder to explain.
Also covers: filter, wrapper and embedded methods; RFE.
From 300 survey questions, selection keeps the 25 most predictive. PCA instead builds 20 new combined scores that capture most of the variation but have no plain-English meaning.
What is PCA, how does it work, and what are its limits?

Principal component analysis finds new axes, the principal components, that are uncorrelated and ordered by how much of the data's variance they capture. Steps: standardise the data, compute the covariance matrix (or use SVD), find its eigenvectors and eigenvalues, keep the top components, and project the data onto them. You choose how many to keep from the cumulative explained variance, for example 95%. It is linear, sensitive to scaling and outliers, and its components are hard to interpret; high variance does not always mean useful for prediction.
Also covers: eigenvectors, explained variance, SVD, multicollinearity remedy.

Forty correlated body measurements reduce to 3 components that explain 92% of variation, roughly 'overall size', 'shape' and 'proportion'. A regression on those 3 avoids the collinearity of the originals.
What are t-SNE and UMAP, and how are they different from PCA?

t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear methods for visualising high-dimensional data in 2D or 3D by keeping neighbours close. PCA is linear, fast, deterministic and gives components you can use as features. t-SNE focuses on local structure, and cluster sizes and distances between clusters in its plots are not meaningful; results depend on the perplexity setting and random seed. UMAP is usually faster and tends to preserve more global structure, and can also transform new data. Use them for exploration, not as proof of clusters.
Plotting 784-pixel handwritten digits with t-SNE shows ten tight groups, a good sign the digits are separable, but the gaps between groups should not be over-read.
What are Weight of Evidence (WoE) and Information Value (IV)?

They are classic credit-scoring tools for turning a variable into binned, monotonic risk scores and ranking its usefulness. For each bin, WoE = ln(share of good outcomes / share of bad outcomes) (sign conventions vary), and IV sums (good share - bad share) x WoE over bins. Commonly quoted rules of thumb: IV below about 0.02 is useless, 0.1 to 0.3 is medium, 0.3 to 0.5 is strong, and above 0.5 is suspiciously strong and worth checking for leakage. They suit logistic scorecards and need care with small bins.
Binning 'age' into 18-25, 26-40 and 41+ and finding WoE falls steadily with age tells you older applicants are consistently lower risk, and the IV tells you how much that variable is worth.
What is the difference between long data and wide data, and how do you reshape it?

Wide data has one row per subject and a column for each measurement (for example one column per month). Long (tidy) data has one row per observation (subject, month, value). Long format is usually better for plotting, grouping and modelling; wide is nicer for reading and some models. In pandas, melt turns wide into long and pivot or pivot_table turns long into wide; in R, pivot_longer and pivot_wider.
Also covers: tidy data.
Monthly sales in columns Jan, Feb, Mar (wide) become rows (store, month, sales) after melt, which makes 'average sales by month' a simple group-by.
What is feature engineering and what are good examples?

Feature engineering is creating inputs that make the pattern easier for the model to see, using domain knowledge. Examples: date parts (day of week, month, is-holiday), ratios (debt to income), aggregates (orders in the last 30 days), counts and recency-frequency-monetary values, interactions, text n-grams, log or power transforms of skewed variables, and binning. Good features often beat fancy models. Every feature must be computable at prediction time with the information available then.
Also covers: interactions, aggregates, transforms for skew (log, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson).
For churn, raw login timestamps are weak. 'Days since last login' and 'logins in the last 14 days divided by the previous 14' are far more predictive.
What is data augmentation and when do you use it?

Data augmentation creates extra training examples by changing existing ones in ways that do not change the label, to reduce overfitting and teach invariances. For images: flips, rotations, crops, colour and lighting changes, noise. For text: synonym replacement, back-translation. For audio: noise, pitch and speed changes. It must fit the task: flipping text images breaks OCR. For tabular data, techniques like SMOTE exist but are riskier.
A pet-photo classifier with 2,000 images gets random flips, small rotations and brightness changes each epoch, which acts like having many more photos and improves validation accuracy.
How do you deal with highly skewed features and high-cardinality categories?

For right-skewed numbers (income, counts) I apply a log or log1p transform, or Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson, which helps linear models and stabilises variance; trees do not care. For categories with thousands of values, I group rare values into 'other', or use frequency or out-of-fold target encoding, hashing, or embeddings. I check each transform on validation data and apply it identically at serving time.
Order value ranges from 1 to 100,000 and is heavily skewed; log1p makes the distribution close to bell-shaped and a linear model's error drops noticeably.
What is ZCA whitening?

Whitening transforms features so they are uncorrelated and have unit variance, meaning the covariance matrix becomes the identity. ZCA (zero-phase component analysis) is the particular whitening that stays as close as possible to the original data, so whitened images still look like images. It removes the first and second-order structure, which can help classifiers on small images, but it is rarely used in modern deep learning, where batch normalisation and large datasets are the norm.
Neighbouring pixels in a photo are highly correlated. ZCA whitening decorrelates them while keeping edges visible, forcing the model to look at what is distinctive.
What is train-serving skew and how do you avoid it?

Train-serving skew is when features are computed differently in training than in production, for example a different code path, a different time window, or a different default for missing values, so a model that tested well behaves badly live. I avoid it by using one shared feature definition (a feature store or a shared library), packaging preprocessing inside the model pipeline, logging served features, and comparing their distributions with training data.
Training computes 'average spend over 30 days' from the warehouse, but the live service computes it from a 7-day cache. The model sees smaller numbers in production and under-predicts.
What is the Central Limit Theorem and why does it matter?

The Central Limit Theorem says that if you take many random samples and compute each sample's mean, those sample means will be approximately normally distributed, centred on the population mean, with standard deviation sigma divided by the square root of n, as long as the samples are independent and the population has finite variance. A sample size of around 30 or more is a common rule of thumb, but heavily skewed data needs more. It matters because it lets us build confidence intervals and run t-tests and z-tests even when the raw data is not normal. It is about sample means, not about the data itself.
Also covers: standard error, assumptions.

Individual delivery times are skewed with a long tail, but the average of 50 randomly chosen deliveries, repeated many times, forms a bell curve, so we can put a confidence interval around the average.
What common probability distributions should a data scientist know?

Normal (bell curve, many natural measurements and sample means); binomial (number of successes in n yes/no trials, like clicks out of visits); multinomial (the same for more than two outcomes, like counts of each die face); Poisson (counts of events in a fixed interval, like calls per hour); uniform (all values equally likely); exponential (waiting time between events); and heavy-tailed ones like log-normal and power law for incomes and web traffic. Knowing the shape guides the model and the test.
Also covers: binomial vs multinomial.
Out of 1,000 visitors with a 3% conversion rate, the number who buy follows a binomial distribution centred on 30. Support calls arriving per hour follow roughly a Poisson distribution.
What are mean, median, mode and standard deviation, and what changes for a sample versus a population?

Mean is the average; median is the middle value and is robust to outliers; mode is the most frequent value. Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean. For a population you divide the squared deviations by N; for a sample you divide by n - 1 (Bessel's correction), because the sample mean is itself estimated from the same data, which would otherwise understate the spread. Use median for skewed data like incomes.
Also covers: variance, Bessel correction, skewness.
Five salaries: 40, 42, 45, 48, 400 (in thousands). The mean is 115k and misleads; the median is 45k and describes the typical person.
What is a p-value, and how is it commonly misunderstood?

The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what you observed if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value says the data would be surprising under the null, so you doubt the null. It is not the probability that the null is true, not the probability the result is due to chance, and not the size or importance of the effect. A threshold such as 0.05 is a convention. Large samples can give tiny p-values for trivial effects, so report effect size and confidence intervals too.
Also covers: significance level, statistical vs practical significance.
A new checkout page lifts conversion from 5.00% to 5.05% across 10 million visits, p < 0.001. It is statistically significant but may not be worth shipping.
Walk me through the steps of hypothesis testing.

State the null hypothesis (no effect or no difference) and the alternative. Choose the significance level alpha, often 0.05, and the test that fits the data. Collect data and compute the test statistic and p-value. If the p-value is below alpha, reject the null; otherwise you fail to reject it, which is not the same as proving it true. Finally report the effect size and a confidence interval and interpret in business terms. Some notes say 'accept the null'; the careful wording is 'fail to reject'.
Also covers: critical value, one- vs two-tailed tests, test statistic.
Null: the new email subject line has the same open rate as the old one. With p = 0.01 at alpha = 0.05, you reject the null and conclude the open rates differ.
What are Type I and Type II errors, and what is statistical power?

A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis (alpha is its probability). A Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject a false null (beta is its probability). Power is 1 - beta, the chance of detecting a real effect, and rises with larger samples, bigger true effects and a higher alpha. Which error is worse depends on context: a medical screen tolerates false alarms to avoid missing disease, while a regulator approving a drug wants to avoid false claims.
Also covers: false positive vs false negative, sample-size planning.
A pregnancy test that says 'pregnant' to someone who is not is a Type I error; one that says 'not pregnant' to someone who is, is Type II.
What is a confidence interval and how do you interpret it?

A 95% confidence interval is a range computed so that if you repeated the study many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value. It is not 'a 95% probability the true value lies in this particular interval' in the strict frequentist reading, though it is commonly paraphrased that way. A narrow interval means a precise estimate; one that includes zero (or no difference) means the effect is not clearly different from nothing. Larger samples shrink it.
Also covers: margin of error, standard error.
A test finds the lift in sign-ups is 2.1% with a 95% interval of 0.4% to 3.8%. The effect is probably positive, but the true value could be small or fairly large.
What are the t-test and z-test, and when do you use each?

Both compare means. The z-test assumes the population standard deviation is known, or the sample is large, and uses the normal distribution. The t-test is for when the standard deviation is estimated from the sample, which is the usual case, and uses the t distribution, which has heavier tails for small samples. Types: one-sample (mean versus a known value), independent two-sample (two groups; Welch's version does not assume equal variances) and paired (same subjects before and after).
Also covers: Welch's t-test, paired vs independent, normality assumptions.

Comparing the average order value of two landing pages with 40 visitors each uses an independent two-sample t-test. Comparing a user's weekly steps before and after an app update uses a paired t-test.
What is the chi-square test and when do you use it?

The chi-square test works on counts in categories. A test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are related (does plan type relate to churn?), by comparing observed counts in a table with the counts expected if they were independent. A goodness-of-fit test asks whether observed counts match an expected distribution (is the die fair?). Expected counts should be reasonably large (a common rule is at least 5 per cell). It is a distribution-free test and does not work on continuous raw values or percentages.
Of 200 free users, 40 upgraded, and of 200 users who got a tutorial, 70 upgraded. A chi-square test checks whether the tutorial and upgrading are associated beyond chance.
What are ANOVA, ANCOVA, MANOVA and MANCOVA?

ANOVA tests whether the means of two or more groups differ by comparing between-group variance to within-group variance with an F-test. If significant, a post-hoc test (like Tukey's) shows which groups differ. ANCOVA adds a continuous covariate to adjust for a nuisance variable. MANOVA handles two or more outcome variables at once. MANCOVA is MANOVA with covariates. ANOVA assumes roughly normal groups, equal variances and independent samples.
Also covers: one-way vs two-way ANOVA, F-test, post-hoc tests.
Comparing average test scores for three teaching methods is one-way ANOVA. Adjusting for each student's prior grade makes it ANCOVA.
What is the F-test?

The F-test compares two variances or, in ANOVA and regression, compares explained variance to unexplained variance. The F statistic is a ratio; if the null is true it is close to 1, and a large value suggests the groups or the model explain more than chance. In regression, the overall F-test asks whether the model as a whole is better than one with no predictors.
In a regression summary an F-statistic of 45 with p < 0.001 says at least one feature is related to the target.
What is the difference between correlation and covariance, and between correlation and causation?

Covariance measures whether two variables move together, but its size depends on the units, so it is hard to compare. Correlation divides by both standard deviations, giving a unit-free value from -1 to 1 for the strength and direction of a linear relationship. Pearson correlation measures linear association; Spearman uses ranks and handles monotonic non-linear relationships and outliers better. Correlation does not imply causation: a third factor (a confounder), reverse causation or coincidence can create it.
Also covers: Pearson vs Spearman, confounders.
Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated because hot weather drives both. Banning ice cream would not reduce drownings.
How would you design and analyse an A/B test?

Define one primary metric and a few guardrail metrics, state the hypothesis, and choose the randomisation unit (usually the user). Use a power calculation to set the sample size from the baseline rate, the smallest effect worth detecting and alpha, and run for whole weekly cycles. Before analysing, check the groups were split as planned (a sample-ratio-mismatch check). Do not stop early when it first looks significant, which inflates false positives, unless you use a sequential method designed for it. Then test, report the effect with an interval, and check segments carefully since many slices create false discoveries.
Also covers: sample size, SRM, peeking, guardrails, novelty effects.
To detect a lift in conversion from 5.0% to 5.5% you may need tens of thousands of users per group. Checking daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05 would make the test misleading.
What is the multiple comparisons problem and how do you handle it?

If you run many tests at alpha = 0.05, some will look significant by chance: with 20 independent tests, the chance of at least one false positive is about 64%. Corrections: Bonferroni (divide alpha by the number of tests; simple but conservative) and Holm, or control the false discovery rate with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, which is common when testing many metrics or genes. Better still, pre-register a small number of hypotheses.
Slicing an A/B test by 40 countries and finding two 'significant' ones is expected noise; apply a correction before celebrating.
What is the difference between frequentist and Bayesian statistics?

Frequentist statistics treats parameters as fixed unknowns and probability as long-run frequency, giving p-values and confidence intervals. Bayesian statistics treats parameters as uncertain, starts with a prior belief, updates it with data to a posterior distribution, and speaks directly about probabilities, such as 'a 94% chance that version B is better'. Bayesian results are easier to interpret and handle small data and prior knowledge, but depend on the prior and can be more computationally demanding.
Also covers: prior, posterior, credible interval.
After an A/B test, a Bayesian report might say 'probability B beats A is 92%, expected lift 1.3%', which is closer to what a product manager wants than a p-value.
What is bootstrapping?

Bootstrapping estimates the uncertainty of any statistic by repeatedly resampling your own data with replacement, recomputing the statistic each time, and looking at the spread of the results. It needs few assumptions and works for medians, ratios and other statistics with no simple formula. It does not rescue a tiny or biased sample, and it fails for some statistics such as extreme values.
To get a confidence interval for the median order value, resample the orders 5,000 times, take each median, and use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the interval.
What is causal inference and how do you get beyond correlation?

Causal inference asks what would happen if we intervened. The gold standard is a randomised experiment, which balances confounders by design. When you cannot randomise, observational methods try to mimic it: adjusting for confounders in a regression, matching or weighting on propensity scores, difference-in-differences (compare changes over time between treated and untreated groups), regression discontinuity, or instrumental variables. They rely on assumptions you cannot fully test, so I state them openly and run sensitivity checks.
Also covers: confounder, treatment effect, propensity score, difference-in-differences.
A company launches a loyalty programme and members spend more. But keen shoppers chose to join, so compare similar customers, or randomly invite some customers to join, to estimate the true effect.
What is Simpson's paradox and what is sampling bias?

Simpson's paradox is when a trend that appears in each group reverses or vanishes when the groups are combined, usually because groups have different sizes and a hidden variable drives both. Sampling bias is when the data collected does not represent the population you care about, such as surveying only people who answer phone calls. Both warn you to check how the data was produced and to break results down by key segments before concluding.
Treatment A has a higher success rate than B for both small and large kidney stones, yet B looks better overall because B was mostly given the easier small-stone cases.
What are non-parametric tests and when would you use them?

Non-parametric tests make few assumptions about the data's distribution, so they suit small samples, ordinal data or heavy skew and outliers. Examples: Mann-Whitney U (two independent groups, instead of a t-test), Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired, instead of a paired t-test), Kruskal-Wallis (several groups, instead of ANOVA) and Spearman correlation. They are more robust but somewhat less powerful when the parametric assumptions actually hold.
Comparing customer satisfaction ratings (1 to 5) between two stores uses Mann-Whitney U, because the ratings are ordinal rather than truly continuous.
What is clustering and how do the main algorithms differ?

Clustering groups similar items without labels. K-means assigns points to the nearest of k centres and moves the centres until stable; it is fast, assumes round clusters of similar size, and needs k. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges, so you can cut it at any level, but it is slower on big data. DBSCAN groups dense regions, finds odd shapes, labels sparse points as noise and needs no k, but struggles with varied densities. Gaussian mixtures give soft, probabilistic memberships.
Also covers: soft vs hard clustering, distance metrics, scaling.

Segmenting 100,000 shoppers by spend and visit frequency: k-means gives 5 clean groups. Detecting hotspots of taxi pickups on a map suits DBSCAN, which finds irregular dense areas and ignores isolated points.
How does k-means work and what is k-means++?

K-means picks k starting centres, assigns every point to its nearest centre, recomputes each centre as the mean of its points, and repeats until assignments stop changing. It minimises within-cluster squared distance but can land in a poor local optimum depending on the start. K-means++ picks the starting centres spread out from each other, which gives better and more stable results, and is the default in scikit-learn. Scale the features first, and remember outliers pull centres.
Also covers: inertia, local optima, n_init.
With k = 3 on customer data, the first pass puts everyone into the nearest of three random centres; after updating the centres a few times, the groups settle into low, medium and high spenders.
How do you choose the number of clusters?

No method is perfect, so combine evidence. The elbow method plots within-cluster error against k and looks for where improvement flattens. The silhouette score measures how close each point is to its own cluster versus the next one (higher is better, max 1). The gap statistic and stability under resampling are alternatives, and BIC works for mixture models. Finally, the clusters must be useful: can the business act on four segments but not on nineteen?
Also covers: elbow method, silhouette score, domain judgement.
Silhouette scores for k = 2, 3, 4, 5 come out 0.41, 0.52, 0.47, 0.38, and the elbow bends near 3. Choose 3, then check the groups make business sense.
What is hierarchical clustering and what is a dendrogram?

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with every point alone and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until one remains. How 'closest' is measured is the linkage (single, complete, average or Ward). The dendrogram is the tree of merges: cutting it at a chosen height gives a number of clusters, so you do not choose k up front. It is intuitive but scales poorly beyond tens of thousands of points.
