Clustering 40 countries by economic indicators, the dendrogram shows which countries merge first; cutting at a height that gives 4 groups yields familiar blocs.
How does DBSCAN work and when would you use it over k-means?

DBSCAN defines clusters as dense regions. A point with at least min_samples neighbours within distance eps is a core point; clusters grow by linking core points and their neighbours, and points in no dense region are labelled noise. It finds arbitrary shapes and flags outliers without choosing k, but it is sensitive to eps and struggles when clusters have very different densities. Use it for spatial data and noisy data.
Two crescent-shaped groups of points defeat k-means, which splits them wrongly, but DBSCAN follows the crescents and labels stray points as noise.
How do you evaluate clustering when there are no labels?

Use internal measures such as the silhouette score, the Davies-Bouldin index (lower is better) and the Calinski-Harabasz index. Check stability by re-clustering on resampled data. If some ground truth exists, external measures such as adjusted Rand index compare clusters to it. In practice also profile each cluster and ask whether it is distinct, explainable and actionable.
Four customer segments with clearly different average basket sizes and visit frequencies are stable across bootstraps, so the team trusts them enough to design offers for each.
What is market basket analysis and how do support, confidence and lift work?

Market basket analysis finds items that are bought together using association rules like milk then butter. Support is how often the combination appears: P(milk and butter). Confidence is how often butter appears given milk: support divided by P(milk). Lift is confidence divided by P(butter); above 1 means the items appear together more than chance, 1 means independent. Algorithms such as Apriori and FP-Growth find frequent itemsets efficiently. In Python, mlxtend is a common library (verify current usage).
Also covers: antecedent and consequent, Apriori, FP-Growth, association analysis uses.

Of 100 customers, 10 bought milk, 8 butter and 6 both. Support = 0.06, confidence of milk to butter = 6/10 = 0.6, and lift = 0.6/0.08 = 7.5, so milk buyers are far more likely than average to buy butter. (A common study note mislabels these.)
How do recommender systems work?

Content-based filtering recommends items similar to what the user liked, using item features. Collaborative filtering uses behaviour of many users: users who liked what you liked also liked X (user-based), or items often liked together (item-based). Matrix factorisation learns hidden factor vectors for users and items so that their dot product predicts a rating or click. Modern systems use two-tower neural networks that embed users and items, retrieve candidates quickly with nearest-neighbour search, then rank them with a richer model. Hybrids combine these.
Also covers: cold start, implicit vs explicit feedback, two-tower retrieval and ranking.

A streaming service finds that viewers who watched your last five films also watched a certain thriller (collaborative), and that this thriller shares genre and director with your favourites (content-based). It recommends the thriller.
How do you handle the cold-start problem and evaluate a recommender?

For new users, show popular or trending items, ask for a few preferences, and use context like location or device; for new items, rely on content features and exploration (such as bandits) so they get shown. Offline, evaluate with precision at k, recall at k, mean average precision and NDCG on held-out interactions, split by time. The decisive test is online: A/B test on click-through, watch time or revenue, plus diversity, novelty and fairness checks, because offline gains do not always carry over.
Also covers: NDCG, bandits, popularity bias.
A new movie with no views is shown to a small random group of fans of its genre; the clicks then give the model data to place it properly.
What approaches exist for anomaly detection?

It depends on whether you have labels. With none: statistical rules (z-score, IQR), distance and density methods such as k-nearest neighbours and local outlier factor, isolation forest (anomalies are isolated in fewer random splits), one-class SVM, and autoencoders that flag inputs they reconstruct badly. With some labels, treat it as imbalanced classification. For time series, compare to a forecast and flag large residuals. The hard parts are defining 'normal', choosing the alert threshold and keeping false alarms tolerable.
Also covers: isolation forest, LOF, autoencoder-based detection.
A payments team trains an autoencoder on normal transactions. A transaction it reconstructs poorly gets a high anomaly score and goes to a fraud analyst for review.
What is customer segmentation with RFM, and how is it done?

RFM scores each customer on Recency (days since last purchase), Frequency (number of purchases) and Monetary value (total spend), often as quintile scores. Combining them gives segments such as champions, loyal, at risk and lost, which need different actions. You can use the scores directly, or cluster on scaled, log-transformed RFM values with k-means. It is simple, explainable and a good first segmentation.
A customer who bought yesterday, ten times this year, spending a lot, is a champion. One who bought heavily two years ago and never since is 'at risk' and gets a win-back offer.
What is active learning and semi-supervised learning?

When labels are expensive, active learning lets the model choose which unlabelled examples are most worth a human labelling (for example the ones it is most uncertain about), so you reach good accuracy with fewer labels. Semi-supervised learning uses a small labelled set plus a lot of unlabelled data, for example by pseudo-labelling confident predictions or by consistency training. Tools such as ALiPy implement many active-learning strategies (verify current maintenance).

A medical imaging team has 100,000 scans and budget to label 2,000. The model keeps asking the radiologist about the scans it is least sure of, reaching the target accuracy with a quarter of the labels.
What is a time series and what are its components?

A time series is data recorded in time order, usually at regular intervals, where the order matters. It is commonly decomposed into level (the baseline), trend (long-term rise or fall), seasonality (repeating patterns at a fixed period such as weekly or yearly), cycles (longer, irregular swings) and noise (what is left). The combination can be additive (components add) or multiplicative (seasonal swings grow with the level). Decomposition methods such as STL separate them.
Also covers: additive vs multiplicative, time series analysis vs forecasting.
Monthly ice-cream sales show an upward trend over years, a summer peak every year (seasonality), and random day-to-day variation (noise).
How is time series forecasting different from ordinary regression?

In time series the order matters and observations are usually correlated with their own past (autocorrelation), which violates the independence that ordinary regression assumes. The goal is usually extrapolating into the future, so validation must respect time: train on the past, test on the future, never shuffle. Features are often lags, rolling statistics and calendar effects. Regression with sensible lag features can still be used, which is how many machine-learning forecasters work.
Predicting next week's sales uses last week's sales, the same week last year and holidays as inputs, and is tested by forecasting weeks the model never saw.
What is stationarity and why does it matter?

A series is (weakly) stationary when its mean, variance and autocorrelation do not change over time: it has no trend or changing spread and no seasonality in its statistical properties. Many classical models such as ARMA assume it, because stable relationships can be learned and extended; a trending series makes estimates and tests unreliable (spurious relationships). If a series is not stationary, transform it first.
Also covers: strict vs weak stationarity, random walk, unit root.
Daily website traffic rising steadily is non-stationary because the mean grows. The day-to-day change in traffic is often stationary.
How do you make a time series stationary and how do you test for it?

Differencing (subtract the previous value; repeat or use seasonal differencing if needed) removes trends. A log or square-root transform stabilises growing variance. Detrending or decomposing and modelling the remainder are other options. Check visually with plots and rolling mean and variance, then with tests: the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test (null: the series has a unit root, i.e. is non-stationary; a small p-value suggests stationarity) and the KPSS test (null: the series is stationary). Do not over-difference.
Also covers: ADF, KPSS, differencing order d, unit root.
Monthly airline passengers grow and swing more over time. Taking logs and then a 12-month seasonal difference gives a series with a flat mean and steady spread.
What are ACF and PACF and how are they used to pick model orders?

The autocorrelation function (ACF) shows the correlation between the series and its lagged copies at each lag. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) shows the correlation at each lag after removing the effect of the shorter lags. A rough guide for a stationary series: a PACF that cuts off after lag p and an ACF that tails off suggests an AR(p) model; an ACF that cuts off after lag q and a PACF that tails off suggests MA(q); both tailing off suggests ARMA. Use information criteria and residual checks to confirm.
Also covers: confidence bands, seasonal spikes.
A PACF with significant spikes at lags 1 and 2 and nothing after, with a slowly decaying ACF, points to an AR(2) starting model.
Explain AR, MA, ARMA and ARIMA.

An autoregressive AR(p) model predicts today from the previous p values. A moving-average MA(q) model predicts today from the previous q forecast errors (not a smoothing average). ARMA(p, q) combines both for stationary series. ARIMA(p, d, q) adds d rounds of differencing to handle trends, so the model works on the differenced series. Choose orders from ACF and PACF or by minimising AIC or BIC, then check residuals look like white noise. Note: the 'moving average' in MA(q) is a model of errors, different from the moving-average smoothing used for charts.
Also covers: lag order, degree of differencing, white-noise residuals.
ARIMA(1,1,1) on monthly sales differences the sales once, then predicts each change from the previous change (AR) and the previous forecast error (MA).
What are SARIMA, SARIMAX and the VAR family?

SARIMA adds seasonal terms (P, D, Q) with a seasonal period m, written ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)m, for data with repeating cycles. SARIMAX also takes exogenous variables, outside inputs such as price or temperature. VAR (vector autoregression) models several series together, where each series depends on its own lags and the lags of the others; VARMA adds moving-average terms and VARMAX adds exogenous inputs. VAR suits connected series such as GDP, inflation and interest rates.
Also covers: exogenous variables, multivariate time series, Granger causality.
Forecasting monthly electricity demand with SARIMAX uses a 12-month season and temperature as an exogenous variable, because heat waves raise demand.
What are moving averages and exponential smoothing?

A simple moving average smooths a series by averaging the last k points, which highlights trends but lags and weights all points equally. Exponential smoothing gives recent points more weight with a smoothing factor alpha between 0 and 1: a bigger alpha reacts quickly, a smaller one is smoother. Simple exponential smoothing handles no trend or seasonality; Holt's method adds trend, and Holt-Winters adds seasonality. These are strong, cheap baselines that often rival complex models.
Also covers: SES, Holt-Winters, smoothing factor.
Forecasting next week's demand with SES, alpha = 0.3: forecast = 0.3 x last week's actual + 0.7 x last week's forecast. Raising alpha makes it chase recent changes.
How do you validate a forecasting model?

Never shuffle. Use a rolling-origin (walk-forward) backtest: train on data up to a date, forecast the next horizon, then move forward and repeat, averaging the errors; scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit does expanding windows. Score with MAE, RMSE, and MAPE or sMAPE (careful with zeros), and MASE to compare to a naive forecast. Always benchmark against a naive baseline (last value, or last season's value). Keep exogenous features available at forecast time to avoid leakage.
Also covers: walk-forward validation, forecast horizon, naive benchmark.
With 3 years of weekly data, train on weeks 1 to 104 and test 105 to 116, then train to 116 and test 117 to 128, and so on. The average error is a realistic estimate.
How are machine learning and deep learning used for forecasting?

A common recipe is to turn forecasting into regression: build lag features, rolling means and calendar features, then train gradient-boosted trees, which are strong and fast. Prophet (an additive trend, seasonality and holiday model) is easy for business series with holidays. Deep learning options include LSTMs, temporal convolution and transformer-based models, which can share patterns across thousands of related series. Newer pre-trained forecasting models also exist; test them on your own data before trusting them. Well-tuned simple methods often win on single series.
Also covers: global vs local models, lag features, Prophet.
A retailer forecasting 50,000 products trains one gradient-boosted model on all of them with features like last week's sales, price and promotion flag, instead of fitting 50,000 separate ARIMAs.
What is a hidden Markov model?

A hidden Markov model describes a system that moves between hidden states following the Markov idea that the next state depends only on the current one, while we only see noisy observations that depend on the state. It is used to infer the most likely hidden sequence (the Viterbi algorithm) and to learn parameters (Baum-Welch, an EM method). Classic uses: speech recognition, part-of-speech tagging and gene finding; today neural networks often replace it, but it is still a good interview concept.
Also covers: Markov assumption, states and emissions.
You cannot see the weather but you see whether a friend carries an umbrella. An HMM infers the likely sequence of sunny and rainy days from the umbrella sightings.
What are AIC and BIC?

Both score how well a model fits while penalising complexity, to balance accuracy and overfitting; lower is better. AIC = 2k - 2 ln(L); BIC = k ln(n) - 2 ln(L), where k is the number of parameters, n the sample size and L the maximised likelihood. BIC penalises extra parameters more, especially for large samples, so it tends to choose simpler models. They compare models fitted to the same data and say nothing about absolute quality.
Candidate ARIMA models give AIC 812, 806 and 809. The second wins, but check its residuals before trusting it.
What is conditional probability, and how does Bayes' theorem work?

Conditional probability P(A given B) is the chance of A once you know B happened: P(A and B) divided by P(B). Bayes' theorem flips it: P(A given B) = P(B given A) x P(A) / P(B). In words: posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence. It is how you update a belief when new evidence arrives, and it is the base of Naive Bayes and Bayesian methods.
Also covers: prior, likelihood, posterior, base-rate fallacy.

A disease affects 1% of people; a test catches 95% of cases and gives 5% false alarms. If you test positive, the chance you are ill is 0.95 x 0.01 / (0.95 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99) = about 16%, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones.
What are independence and conditional independence, and why does Naive Bayes assume them?

Two events are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Conditional independence means that independence holds once you fix a third variable. Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class, which is rarely true but makes the maths simple and often works well enough for ranking classes.
Words like 'free' and 'winner' in a spam email are clearly related, yet treating them as independent given 'spam' still gives a decent classifier.
What are expectation, variance, standard deviation, covariance and correlation?

Expectation is the long-run average of a random variable. Variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and standard deviation is its square root, in the original units. Covariance measures whether two variables move together, but its size depends on units. Correlation is covariance divided by both standard deviations, so it lies between -1 and 1. Correlation measures linear association only and does not prove causation.
Also covers: Pearson vs Spearman, covariance matrix, outliers.
Height in centimetres and in inches have different covariances with weight but the same correlation. A perfect U-shaped relationship can have correlation near zero.
Which probability distributions should a data scientist know, and when does each appear?

Bernoulli: one yes/no trial. Binomial: number of successes in n independent trials. Poisson: count of events in a fixed interval when events are rare and independent. Exponential: waiting time between Poisson events. Uniform: all values equally likely. Normal: sums and averages of many small effects. Log-normal: positive, right-skewed quantities like income. Beta: a probability itself, common in Bayesian A/B tests. Learn the mean and variance of the main ones.
Also covers: geometric, gamma, Student's t, chi-square.
Calls arriving at a help desk per hour are roughly Poisson; the minutes between calls are roughly exponential; the share of visitors who convert has a Beta posterior.
What is the law of large numbers, and how is it different from the central limit theorem?

The law of large numbers says the sample average gets closer to the true mean as the sample grows. The central limit theorem says more: the distribution of that average becomes approximately normal, with spread (the standard error) equal to the standard deviation divided by the square root of n. The first is about where the average lands; the second is about how it varies around it. Heavy-tailed data may need very large samples.
Also covers: standard error, sampling distribution.
Averaging 1,000 coin-flip proportions lands near 0.5 (law of large numbers), and the histogram of many such averages looks like a bell curve (central limit theorem).
What is maximum likelihood estimation, and how does it differ from MAP?

Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) picks the parameters that make the observed data most probable. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) also multiplies in a prior belief about the parameters, so it picks the most probable parameters given data and prior. MAP with a Gaussian prior is the same as L2 regularization, and with a Laplace prior it matches L1. Many loss functions come from MLE: squared error from Gaussian noise, cross-entropy from Bernoulli or categorical outcomes.
Also covers: log-likelihood, why we take logs, regularization as a prior.
Fitting a coin's bias: 7 heads in 10 flips gives an MLE of 0.7. With a prior that favours fair coins, MAP gives something closer to 0.5.
Explain Bayesian versus frequentist thinking.

Frequentists treat parameters as fixed and talk about how often a method would be right over repeated samples (p-values, confidence intervals). Bayesians treat parameters as uncertain, start with a prior, update with data, and report a posterior distribution (credible intervals). Bayesian methods give direct statements like 'there is a 94% chance variant B is better' and handle small data with sensible priors; frequentist methods are simpler and need no prior. Both are used in practice.
Also covers: credible vs confidence interval, priors, posterior.
A 95% confidence interval does not mean there is a 95% chance the true value lies in it; a 95% Bayesian credible interval does mean that, under the chosen prior.
What is statistical power, and how do you pick a sample size?

Power is the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size, equal to 1 minus the Type II error rate. It rises with a larger sample, a bigger true effect, lower noise, and a higher significance level. To choose a sample size, fix the smallest effect worth detecting, the significance level (often 0.05), the desired power (often 0.8), and the variance estimate, then calculate n with a power-analysis tool. Do this before the experiment, not after.
Also covers: minimum detectable effect, alpha, beta, underpowered tests.
To detect a lift from 10% to 11% conversion with 80% power at 5% significance needs thousands of users per group; trying with 200 users will usually miss it.
What is the multiple-comparisons problem, and how do you handle it?

If you run many tests at the 5% level, some will look significant by chance: 20 independent tests give about a 64% chance of at least one false positive. Fixes: Bonferroni (divide the threshold by the number of tests; simple, conservative), Holm (a less conservative step-down version), or control the false discovery rate with Benjamini-Hochberg when you can accept a small share of false findings among many. Also decide the metrics in advance.
Also covers: false discovery rate, p-hacking, pre-registration.
Testing 30 metrics in an A/B test and celebrating the one with p = 0.03 is a trap; with Bonferroni the threshold becomes 0.05 / 30 = about 0.0017.
What is the bootstrap, and when would you use it?

The bootstrap estimates uncertainty by resampling your own data with replacement many times, recomputing the statistic each time, and looking at how it varies. It gives standard errors and confidence intervals for almost any statistic (median, AUC, a ratio) without a formula. It struggles with very small samples, extreme tails, and dependent data such as time series unless adapted.
Also covers: resampling, percentile intervals, permutation tests.
To get a confidence interval for a model's AUC on 2,000 test rows, resample the rows 1,000 times, compute AUC each time, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
How do the t-test, chi-square test, ANOVA and non-parametric tests differ, and how do you choose?

Compare means of two groups: t-test (Welch's version if variances differ; paired t-test for before/after on the same units). Compare means of three or more groups: ANOVA, followed by post-hoc tests. Test association between two categorical variables: chi-square test. If data are far from normal or very small, use rank-based tests such as Mann-Whitney U or Wilcoxon. Always check assumptions and report the effect size, not just the p-value.
Also covers: Z-test, F-test, Kruskal-Wallis, effect size.
Comparing average order value across three pricing pages is ANOVA; whether purchase (yes/no) depends on device type is a chi-square test.
What assumptions does linear regression make, and how do you check them?

Linearity of the relationship, independent errors, constant error variance (homoscedasticity), approximately normal errors (mainly matters for inference on small samples), and little multicollinearity. Check with residual plots against fitted values (curves suggest non-linearity, a funnel suggests heteroscedasticity), a Q-Q plot, the Durbin-Watson statistic for autocorrelation, and VIF for multicollinearity. Remedies: transformations, extra features, robust standard errors, or a different model.
Also covers: Q-Q plot, Durbin-Watson, robust errors.
House prices whose residuals fan out for expensive homes suggest heteroscedasticity; modelling log(price) often fixes it.
What does the p-value not tell you, and how should results be reported?

A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, not the size or importance of an effect, and not a measure of reproducibility. With huge samples, trivial effects become 'significant'; with tiny samples, real effects are missed. Report the effect size with a confidence interval, the sample size, how many tests you ran, and the practical meaning in business terms.
Also covers: statistical vs practical significance, replication.
A 0.1% lift with p < 0.001 on 50 million users is statistically significant but may not cover the cost of the change.
What are bias, variance and consistency of an estimator, and what is the bias-variance decomposition?

An estimator is unbiased if its average over many samples equals the true value; its variance is how much it fluctuates; it is consistent if it converges to the truth as the sample grows. A model's expected squared error splits into bias squared (systematic error), variance (sensitivity to the training sample) and irreducible noise. Slight bias can pay off when it cuts variance a lot, which is why regularization helps.
Also covers: sample variance with n minus 1, shrinkage.
Dividing by n - 1 instead of n when computing sample variance corrects a small downward bias in the estimate.
What is Simpson's paradox, and what do selection and survivorship bias look like in data?

Simpson's paradox is when a trend in every subgroup reverses once the groups are combined, because group sizes differ and a hidden variable matters. Selection bias is when the data you have is not representative of the population you care about; survivorship bias is a form of it where you only see the cases that survived a filter. Fix by thinking about how the data was generated and stratifying or adjusting for the hidden variable.
Also covers: confounding, sampling bias, missing-not-at-random.
A treatment can look worse overall than another while being better for both mild and severe patients, if it was mostly given to severe patients.

s.t: Linear algebra, calculus and information theory
q: Why do vectors, matrices and matrix multiplication matter in machine learning?

Data is a matrix (rows are examples, columns are features); a linear layer is a matrix multiply plus a bias; embeddings are vectors; and whole batches are processed at once as large matrix products, which GPUs do very fast. Key facts: multiplication is not commutative, (AB) transposed is B-transposed times A-transposed, and the shapes must match, (m x n) times (n x p) gives (m x p). Shape errors are among the most common bugs.
Also covers: dot product, transpose, shapes, broadcasting.
A batch of 32 inputs with 100 features multiplied by a 100 x 10 weight matrix gives a 32 x 10 output: ten scores for each of 32 examples.
What are eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and where do they appear in data science?

An eigenvector of a matrix is a direction that the matrix only stretches or flips, never rotates; the eigenvalue is the stretch factor. For a covariance matrix, eigenvectors are the principal directions of variation and eigenvalues say how much variance lies along each, which is exactly PCA. They also appear in spectral clustering, PageRank, and stability analysis.
Also covers: covariance matrix, principal components, spectral methods.
In PCA, the first eigenvector of the covariance matrix is the line through the data cloud along which the points are most spread out.
What is the singular value decomposition (SVD), and what is it used for?

SVD factors any matrix into three parts: rotation, scaling (singular values), and another rotation. Keeping only the largest singular values gives the best low-rank approximation. Uses: PCA computed stably, recommender systems and matrix factorisation, latent semantic analysis for text, image compression and noise removal, and the idea behind LoRA-style low-rank updates in language models.
Also covers: low-rank approximation, truncated SVD, rank.
A ratings matrix of users by movies can be approximated by a few 'taste' factors, which is how early recommender systems predicted missing ratings.
What are the L1, L2 and Frobenius norms, and why do they matter?

A norm measures the size of a vector. L1 is the sum of absolute values, L2 is the usual straight-line length (square root of the sum of squares), and the Frobenius norm is the L2 norm applied to all entries of a matrix. They define regularization penalties (L1 gives sparse solutions, L2 shrinks smoothly), distance measures such as Manhattan and Euclidean, and gradient clipping.
Also covers: Manhattan, Euclidean, cosine similarity.
Weight decay adds a penalty proportional to the squared L2 norm of the weights to the loss, pulling weights toward zero.
What are derivatives, gradients, the chain rule, the Jacobian and the Hessian?

A derivative is the slope of a function; a gradient collects the slopes with respect to every input and points toward steepest increase, so training steps go the opposite way. The chain rule multiplies derivatives through composed functions, which is exactly how backpropagation works. The Jacobian is the matrix of first derivatives of a vector function; the Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives and describes curvature, used in second-order optimisation but too costly for large networks.
Also covers: partial derivative, automatic differentiation, curvature.
For loss = (w x - y) squared, the gradient with respect to w is 2 (w x - y) x; if the prediction is too high, the gradient is positive and the update lowers w.
What is a convex function, and why does it matter for optimisation?

A function is convex if a straight line between any two points on its curve never goes below the curve, so it has a single basin: any local minimum is the global minimum. Linear and logistic regression have convex losses, so gradient descent reliably finds the best weights. Neural network losses are non-convex with many saddle points and local minima, yet good optimisers still find solutions that generalise well.
Also covers: local vs global minimum, saddle points.
Fitting a straight line by least squares always has one best answer; training a deep network from different random starts gives different but similarly good weights.
What is entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence?

Entropy measures uncertainty in a distribution: the average surprise. Cross-entropy is the average surprise when you use distribution Q to encode data that really comes from P; as a loss it punishes confident wrong predictions heavily. KL divergence is cross-entropy minus entropy, the extra cost of using Q instead of P; it is not symmetric, so it is not a true distance. Minimising cross-entropy against fixed labels is the same as maximising likelihood.
Also covers: log loss, information gain, Jensen-Shannon divergence.
If a model gives 0.9 probability to the correct class, the loss is about 0.105 (the negative log of 0.9); at 0.1 it is about 2.3, a far heavier penalty.
What is mutual information, and how is it used for feature selection?

Mutual information measures how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another. Unlike correlation, it captures non-linear relationships and works with categorical variables. For feature selection, rank features by mutual information with the target and keep the top ones. It estimates relevance only, so redundant features can both score high; combine it with checks for correlation between features.
Day of week may have zero correlation with sales yet high mutual information if sales follow a non-linear weekly cycle.
Why do we work with log-probabilities and the softmax in a numerically stable way?

Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to zero, so we add their logs instead. Softmax uses exponentials that can overflow for large scores, so implementations subtract the largest score first, which does not change the result. Libraries offer combined, stable functions such as log-softmax with cross-entropy, so use those rather than computing the pieces yourself.
Also covers: underflow, overflow, log-sum-exp.
Scores of 1000, 1001, 1002 would overflow in exp; subtracting 1002 gives 0, -1 and -2, which are safe and give the same probabilities.
How do you design and analyse a good A/B test?

Define one primary metric and guardrail metrics, the smallest effect worth detecting, and the sample size from a power calculation. Randomise by the right unit (usually the user), check the groups are balanced and that the traffic split matches the plan (sample ratio mismatch), run for whole weeks to cover weekly cycles, and do not stop early because the result looks good. Analyse with a test suited to the metric, report effect size and interval, and consider novelty effects and whether the result generalises.
Also covers: guardrail metrics, sample ratio mismatch, novelty effect, unit of randomisation.
A new checkout button lifts conversion in week one because it is new; by week three the lift fades. Running longer exposed the novelty effect.
Why is peeking at an A/B test a problem, and what are the fixes?

Checking the p-value repeatedly and stopping when it first dips below 0.05 inflates false positives far above 5%. Fixes: commit to a fixed sample size and look once; use sequential testing methods designed for continuous monitoring (such as alpha-spending or always-valid p-values); or use a Bayesian approach with decision rules set in advance. Platforms differ in what they support, so check what your tool actually does.
Also covers: sequential testing, alpha spending, optional stopping.
Checking daily for 14 days and stopping at the first p below 0.05 can push the real false-positive rate to well above 20% for tests with no true effect.
What is CUPED, and how can you make experiments more sensitive?

CUPED (controlled-experiment using pre-experiment data) reduces variance by adjusting each user's metric using a correlated pre-experiment measurement, such as their spend before the test. Lower variance means smaller needed samples or faster decisions. Other options: stratified sampling, choosing a less noisy metric, trimming extreme outliers, and triggered analysis that only counts users who saw the change.
Also covers: variance reduction, stratification, triggered analysis.
If a user's past spend predicts their spend during the test, subtracting that predictable part leaves a cleaner treatment signal.
What are confounders, and what is the difference between correlation and causation?

A confounder influences both the treatment and the outcome, creating an association that is not causal. Correlation shows variables move together; causation means changing one changes the other. Randomised experiments break confounding because assignment is random. Without them, you need adjustment (controlling for confounders), careful design, or quasi-experimental methods, and you must state your assumptions.
Also covers: lurking variable, randomised controlled trial, observational data.
Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer; heat is the confounder, and banning ice cream would not reduce drownings.
What are difference-in-differences, propensity scores, and instrumental variables?

These are quasi-experimental tools for when you cannot randomise. Difference-in-differences compares the before/after change in a treated group with the change in a similar untreated group, assuming they would have moved in parallel. Propensity-score methods model the chance of getting treatment from observed features and then match or weight units to balance groups. Instrumental variables use something that affects treatment but affects the outcome only through it. Each rests on assumptions you cannot fully test.
Also covers: parallel trends, matching, weighting, regression discontinuity.
To measure a feature launched in one city only, compare sales growth in that city with similar cities that did not get it.
What are A/B testing pitfalls with network effects, and how do you handle them?

When users affect each other (marketplaces, social networks), treatment leaks to the control group and the measured effect is biased. Options: randomise by cluster (whole cities or friend groups), switchback tests that alternate treatment over time in a region, or model the interference. Expect lower power with clusters and plan sample size accordingly.
Also covers: interference, switchback tests, cluster randomisation.
A ride-sharing discount given to half the riders also changes driver availability for everyone, so a city-by-week switchback is safer than a rider-level split.
What is uplift modelling?

Uplift modelling predicts the incremental effect of an action on each person, not just who will convert. It helps target only those who are persuadable and avoids spending on people who would buy anyway or who react badly. It needs data from a randomised experiment and is harder to evaluate than ordinary classification (use uplift or Qini curves).
Also covers: persuadables, sure things, lost causes, sleeping dogs.
A discount sent to customers who would have bought anyway wastes money; uplift modelling aims it at those whose purchase probability actually rises.
Why use deep learning instead of classical machine learning, and when not to?

Deep learning learns useful features by itself from raw data such as pixels, audio and text, so you do not hand-craft them, and it improves with large data and compute. It is the right tool for images, speech, language and other unstructured data. For small tabular datasets, classical models such as gradient boosting usually match or beat it, train faster, and are easier to explain. Deep learning needs more data, more compute, careful tuning and is harder to interpret.
Also covers: ML vs DL differences, feature learning, GPUs.
To spot defects in photos of circuit boards, a CNN learns the visual cues itself. To predict churn from a 30-column customer table, gradient boosting is quicker to build and just as accurate.
What is a perceptron and how does it relate to a biological neuron?

A perceptron takes several inputs, multiplies each by a weight, adds them with a bias, and passes the result through an activation function to produce an output. It is loosely inspired by a neuron that collects signals through dendrites, sums them in the cell body and fires along the axon. A single perceptron is a linear classifier; stacking many in layers with non-linear activations gives a neural network that can learn complex patterns. The biological analogy is only loose.
Also covers: weights, bias, multilayer perceptron.
A perceptron for 'approve the loan?' takes income, debt and credit history, weights them, and outputs yes or no. Many of these in layers form a neural network.
What are activation functions and why do we need non-linear ones?

An activation function is applied to a neuron's weighted sum to decide its output. Without non-linear activations, any number of stacked layers collapses into one linear function, no more powerful than linear regression. Common choices: sigmoid (output 0 to 1, used for binary probabilities, prone to vanishing gradients), tanh (output -1 to 1, zero-centred), ReLU (max of 0 and x, simple and fast, the default in hidden layers, but neurons can 'die'), Leaky ReLU (fixes dying), GELU (common in transformers) and softmax (turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1 at the output of a classifier).
Also covers: sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, softmax, dying ReLU.

A network that recognises cats needs to bend and combine features such as edges and textures. ReLU after each layer lets it build those curved decisions; without it the network could only draw straight boundaries.
What is forward propagation and how do depth and width matter?

Forward propagation passes the input through the layers: each layer multiplies by weights, adds biases, applies the activation, and hands the result on until the output layer gives a prediction. Depth is the number of hidden layers and width is the number of units per layer. Deeper networks can build hierarchical features (edges, then shapes, then objects) but are harder to train, while wider layers add capacity per level. There is no rule that always deeper is better; choose by validation performance and training stability.
In a digit classifier, 784 pixel values flow into 128 hidden units, then 64, then 10 output scores, one per digit.
What loss functions are used for regression and classification?

A loss function measures how wrong a prediction is and is what training minimises. For regression: mean squared error, mean absolute error, and Huber loss, which is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones. For binary classification: binary cross-entropy (log loss) with a sigmoid output. For multi-class: categorical cross-entropy with a softmax output. Other losses include hinge loss for SVM-style margins, and contrastive or triplet losses for learning embeddings. Pick the loss that matches the output and the cost of errors.
Also covers: negative log-likelihood, margin losses, why not MSE for classification.
A model gives a 0.9 probability that an email is spam when it is not. Cross-entropy punishes that confident mistake heavily, pushing the network to be better calibrated.
What is backpropagation?

Backpropagation is how a neural network learns. After a forward pass computes the loss, it uses the chain rule of calculus to work out how much each weight contributed to the error, moving backward from the output layer to the first, producing the gradient for every weight. An optimiser then nudges each weight in the direction that reduces the loss. It is efficient because it reuses intermediate results; deep learning frameworks do it automatically (autograd).
Also covers: chain rule, gradient, automatic differentiation.

A network predicts 0.2 where the answer is 1. Backprop tells the last layer's weights to increase, then tells the earlier layers how much their weights influenced that last layer, so every weight is nudged a little in the right direction.
Explain batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent.

Gradient descent repeatedly moves the weights a small step against the gradient of the loss. Batch gradient descent computes the gradient on the whole dataset each step: stable but slow and memory-heavy. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses one example per step: fast, noisy updates that can help escape poor spots. Mini-batch uses a small group (like 32 to 512 examples), the standard compromise: efficient on GPUs and less noisy than pure SGD. The step size is set by the learning rate.
Also covers: gradient, learning rate, convergence.
With 1 million images, a batch step would process all of them before updating once. Mini-batches of 256 update the weights about 4,000 times per pass, which learns much faster.
What are optimisers such as momentum, RMSProp and Adam, and which is best?

Optimisers decide how to use the gradient. Momentum accumulates a running average of gradients to speed along consistent directions and smooth noise. RMSProp divides by a running average of recent squared gradients so each weight gets its own adaptive step size. Adam combines momentum and RMSProp and is a popular default; AdamW fixes how weight decay is applied and is common for transformers. There is no single best: Adam usually converges fast with little tuning, while SGD with momentum and a good schedule is often preferred for some vision models. Test on your problem.
Also covers: Adam, AdamW, SGD with momentum, adaptive learning rates.
Training a language model usually starts with AdamW and a learning-rate warm-up. Training a ResNet on images often does well with SGD, momentum 0.9 and a step or cosine schedule.
What is the learning rate and how do you choose and schedule it?

The learning rate sets the size of each update. Too high and the loss bounces or diverges; too low and training is painfully slow or gets stuck. It is usually the most important hyperparameter. Run a short learning-rate range test, then use a schedule: warm-up at the start, then decay (step, exponential or cosine) or reduce on plateau. Cyclical and one-cycle schedules are also used. Larger batch sizes often allow larger learning rates. The common claim that learning rates are 'randomly initialised' is wrong; you set them.
Also covers: warm-up, cosine decay, reduce on plateau.
If the loss shoots to NaN in the first few steps, divide the learning rate by 10. If it falls very slowly, try 3 times larger.
What are epochs, batch size and iterations?

One epoch is one full pass over the training data. The batch size is the number of examples used for each weight update, and an iteration is one update, so iterations per epoch = dataset size divided by batch size. Too few epochs underfit; too many overfit, so use early stopping on a validation set (more epochs do not always mean better accuracy). Small batches give noisier, sometimes better-generalising updates; big batches use hardware well but may need a higher learning rate. Memory limits the batch size.
With 50,000 images and a batch size of 100, one epoch is 500 iterations. Training for 20 epochs is 10,000 weight updates.
How should weights and biases be initialised?

Starting every weight at zero makes all neurons in a layer compute and learn the same thing (they stay symmetric), so initial weights must be random. Scale matters: too large and signals and gradients blow up, too small and they vanish. Xavier (Glorot) initialisation keeps variance steady and suits tanh or sigmoid; He initialisation uses a variance of 2 divided by the number of inputs and suits ReLU. Biases are usually initialised to zero because random weights already break symmetry.
Also covers: Xavier, He, symmetry breaking.
A 20-layer ReLU network with weights drawn from a plain standard normal distribution can output huge numbers; with He initialisation the activations stay in a sensible range from layer to layer.
What are vanishing and exploding gradients, and how do you fix them?

During backpropagation the gradient is multiplied through many layers. If the factors are mostly less than 1 (typical with sigmoid or tanh), the gradient shrinks to almost zero in early layers, so they stop learning; if they are above 1, it explodes. Fixes: ReLU-style activations, good initialisation (He or Xavier), batch or layer normalisation, residual (skip) connections, gated units such as LSTM in recurrent networks, and gradient clipping for explosions. A shallower network or a lower learning rate can also help.
Also covers: gradient clipping, residual connections, LSTM.
In a 30-layer sigmoid network, early layers get gradients around 1e-12 and barely change. Switching to ReLU with residual connections lets the gradient flow and training succeeds.
What is dropout and how does it prevent overfitting?

During training, dropout randomly switches off each neuron with a probability such as 0.5, so the network cannot rely on any single neuron or fragile co-adaptations and must learn more robust features. It acts like training and averaging many thinned networks. At prediction time dropout is turned off and the activations are scaled so their expected size is consistent (modern implementations scale during training, called inverted dropout). It was popularised by Hinton's group; it is applied to hidden layers, not usually to the output layer, and it slows convergence somewhat.
Also covers: keep probability, inverted dropout, regularization.
A dense layer with dropout 0.3 randomly ignores 30% of its units on each training step. The model trains slightly slower but its validation accuracy is higher because it overfits less.
What is batch normalisation and how does it differ from layer normalisation?

Batch normalisation standardises each layer's inputs using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift. It stabilises and speeds up training, allows higher learning rates and acts as a mild regulariser. It depends on batch statistics, so it behaves differently at small batch sizes and at inference (running averages are used). Layer normalisation normalises across the features of each single example, independent of batch size, and is standard in transformers and recurrent networks.
A CNN trained with batch norm reaches the same accuracy in about half the epochs. A transformer uses layer norm because its batches and sequence lengths vary.
What other regularisation techniques are used in deep learning?

Weight decay (an L2 penalty on weights), early stopping on validation loss, data augmentation, dropout, label smoothing, mixup, stochastic depth and, most simply, more data or a smaller model. Ensembling several networks also reduces variance. Combine a few and check on validation data; too much regularisation underfits.
A small image classifier overfits after 12 epochs. Adding flips and crops, weight decay of 1e-4 and early stopping with patience 5 lifts validation accuracy by several points.
How do you tune hyperparameters in deep learning?

Start with a baseline that overfits a tiny subset (a sanity check), then tune the learning rate first, then batch size, depth or width, regularisation and the schedule. Watch training and validation curves in the first few epochs for signs of underfitting or overfitting. Random search beats grid search when only a few parameters matter; tools such as Optuna, Ray Tune, Keras Tuner and Weights and Biases sweeps automate this (verify current features). Track every run so results are reproducible.
Also covers: experiment tracking, short runs, early signals.
Running 20 short 3-epoch trials with random learning rates between 1e-5 and 1e-1 often reveals a good range within an hour before committing to a long run.
Why are deep learning models called black boxes, and how can you explain them?

A network has millions or billions of weights interacting non-linearly, so no human can read the logic, and it is hard to trace why it made a given decision. That matters for safety, fairness and regulation. Tools: feature attribution such as SHAP and LIME, gradient-based saliency maps and Grad-CAM for images (which parts of an image drove the prediction), counterfactual explanations, and simpler surrogate models. Attention weights are not a guaranteed explanation. Explanations should be validated, not just trusted.
Also covers: Explainable AI, Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME.
A skin-lesion classifier highlights, via Grad-CAM, the ruler placed beside lesions in the training photos. The explanation reveals the model learned the ruler, not the lesion.
What is transfer learning and how do you fine-tune a pre-trained model?

Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large task as the starting point for a related one. Early layers learn general features (edges, textures, word patterns) that carry across tasks. You either freeze the pre-trained layers and train a new final layer (feature extraction), or unfreeze some or all layers and train with a small learning rate (fine-tuning), sometimes unfreezing gradually. It lets you get strong results with little data and compute. It works best when the new task resembles the original; it is a different idea from multi-task learning, though some notes confuse them.
Also covers: pre-trained models, freezing layers, discriminative learning rates.

With 800 labelled photos of your product types, take a ResNet pre-trained on ImageNet, replace its last layer and fine-tune for a few epochs. You reach accuracy that training from scratch would need tens of thousands of images for.
What are autoencoders and variational autoencoders?

An autoencoder is a network trained to reproduce its input through a narrow middle layer, so the encoder compresses the data into a short code and the decoder rebuilds it. It learns a compact representation, useful for dimensionality reduction, denoising and anomaly detection (bad reconstruction signals something unusual). Variants: denoising (input is corrupted on purpose), sparse and contractive. A variational autoencoder learns a smooth probability distribution over the code, so you can sample it to generate new data. Compared with PCA, autoencoders can learn non-linear compression.
Also covers: encoder, bottleneck, decoder, reconstruction loss.
Train an autoencoder on normal factory sensor readings. A new reading that it reconstructs with a large error is flagged as a possible fault.
What are GANs, and how do they relate to diffusion models?

A generative adversarial network trains two networks against each other: a generator that makes fake samples and a discriminator that tries to tell real from fake. As each improves, the fakes become realistic. GANs can be unstable to train and may suffer mode collapse (producing a narrow range of outputs). Conditional GANs such as Pix2Pix translate one image into another. Diffusion models, which learn to remove noise step by step, have largely taken over high-quality image generation because they train more stably, though they are slower to sample.
Also covers: generator, discriminator, mode collapse, conditional GAN.
A GAN trained on face photos produces images of people who do not exist. A diffusion model given a text prompt starts from noise and gradually denoises it into a picture.
What are few-shot and meta-learning?

Meta-learning, or learning to learn, trains a model across many tasks so that it can pick up a new task from very few examples. Few-shot learning is the goal: learn from a handful of examples per class. Approaches include metric-based (compare to examples in an embedding space), optimisation-based such as MAML, and, in modern practice, large pre-trained models that can do tasks from a few prompt examples (in-context learning). It is different from one-shot learning, which is the case of a single example.
A support team has only 5 labelled tickets for a brand-new category. A pre-trained embedding model plus those 5 examples can already classify new tickets reasonably well.
How does a convolutional neural network work?

A CNN slides small learnable filters across the image; each filter computes a dot product with the patch under it and produces a feature map showing where that pattern appears. Because the same filter is reused everywhere, there are far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer and the network detects a pattern wherever it occurs. Typical stack: convolution, then an activation such as ReLU, then pooling to shrink the map, repeated, then fully connected (or global pooling) layers that output class scores. Early layers find edges; deeper layers find shapes and objects.
Also covers: feature maps, parameter sharing, local connectivity.
A 32 x 32 x 3 image passed through 12 filters with 'same' padding gives a 32 x 32 x 12 volume; 2 x 2 max pooling with stride 2 reduces it to 16 x 16 x 12.
Explain padding, stride, pooling and how to compute a convolution's output size.

Padding adds a border (usually zeros) so edges are processed and size is preserved ('same'); with none ('valid') the map shrinks. Stride is how far the filter moves each step; larger stride shrinks the output. Pooling downsamples a map, with max pooling keeping the strongest response in each window and average pooling taking the mean, reducing computation and giving some tolerance to small shifts; it works on each channel separately and does not change depth. Output size = floor((W - F + 2P) / S) + 1, for input width W, filter F, padding P and stride S.
Also covers: max vs average pooling, global average pooling.
A 32-pixel input with a 5-pixel filter, padding 0 and stride 1 gives (32 - 5)/1 + 1 = 28 pixels, so a 28 x 28 output.
How does a CNN differ from an RNN?

A CNN uses shared filters over a grid-like input (images, also 1D signals) and is best at spatial patterns; it processes the whole input in parallel. An RNN processes a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward as memory, so it suits ordered data such as text or time series and can handle variable lengths, but it trains sequentially and struggles with long-range dependencies. Transformers have largely replaced RNNs for language, and are increasingly used for images too.
Classifying a photo uses a CNN. Predicting the next word of a sentence used to use an RNN and now typically uses a transformer.
How did CNN architectures evolve from LeNet to modern models?

LeNet-5 (1998) read handwritten digits with a few conv and pooling layers. AlexNet (2012) won ImageNet by a wide margin using a deeper network, ReLU, dropout, data augmentation and GPUs, which started the deep-learning boom. VGG (2014) showed that stacking small 3 x 3 filters works. GoogLeNet (2014) introduced inception modules with parallel filter sizes and 1 x 1 convolutions for efficiency. ResNet (2015) added skip connections that let networks reach 100+ layers. Later: DenseNet, EfficientNet (balanced scaling of depth, width and resolution) and vision transformers (2020).
Also covers: ZFNet, GoogLeNet, ImageNet winners, NAS.
ImageNet top-5 error fell from about 26% before 2012 to about 16% with AlexNet in 2012 and to roughly 3.6% with ResNet in 2015 (approximate figures; verify against the papers).
What is VGG16 and what is its main idea?

VGG16 is a 16-weight-layer CNN from Oxford (2014) built only from 3 x 3 convolutions with stride 1 and 2 x 2 max pooling with stride 2, followed by three fully connected layers. The idea: two stacked 3 x 3 convolutions cover the same area as one 5 x 5 but with fewer parameters (18 versus 25 per channel pair) and an extra non-linearity. Its simplicity makes it a popular feature extractor, but it has about 138 million parameters, which is heavy.
Teams still use VGG-style features for image similarity or style transfer because the layers are easy to understand, even though lighter networks are more efficient.
What is ResNet and why do skip connections help?

A residual network adds a shortcut that passes a block's input straight to its output, so the block only has to learn the residual change. This gives gradients a direct path back through the network, which fixes the degradation problem where very deep plain networks got worse, even on training data. ResNet won ImageNet 2015 with 152 layers and made very deep networks routine. The skip connection is an identity shortcut, not a recurrent gate, despite some notes saying so.
Also covers: degradation problem, identity shortcut, bottleneck block.
A 34-layer plain network had higher training error than an 18-layer one; the 34-layer ResNet had lower training error than its 18-layer version, showing the shortcut solves the depth problem.
What are inception modules and 1x1 convolutions?

An inception module applies several filter sizes (1x1, 3x3, 5x5) and pooling in parallel on the same input and concatenates the results, letting the network choose the scale. A 1x1 convolution mixes channels at each position and is used to reduce the number of channels before expensive larger filters, cutting parameters and computation. GoogLeNet used these plus global average pooling instead of large fully connected layers, ending with far fewer parameters than AlexNet. (GoogLeNet itself did not use batch normalisation; that came with later Inception versions.)
A 1x1 convolution that shrinks 256 channels to 64 before a 3x3 convolution makes that 3x3 step about four times cheaper.
What is ImageNet and why is it important?

ImageNet is a large labelled image database organised by WordNet categories, with millions of images across thousands of categories. The ILSVRC challenge, based on a 1,000-class subset with about 1.2 million training images, was the main benchmark for image classification from 2010 to 2017, and models pre-trained on it became the default starting point for transfer learning. Its bias and labelling issues are now well known.
Most 'pre-trained' vision weights you download, such as ResNet-50, were trained on ImageNet-1k, and you fine-tune them for your own classes.
How does object detection work, from R-CNN to Faster R-CNN?

Object detection finds what is in an image and where, by predicting boxes and labels. R-CNN used selective search to propose about 2,000 regions and ran a CNN on each, which was accurate but very slow. Fast R-CNN ran the CNN once on the whole image and pooled features per region. Faster R-CNN added a region proposal network that predicts boxes from anchors on the shared features, making proposals nearly free. These are two-stage detectors: propose, then classify and refine.
Also covers: region proposals, anchors, selective search.
In a street photo, Faster R-CNN proposes candidate boxes, then classifies each as car, person or background and tightens the box around it.
What is YOLO and how do one-stage detectors differ from two-stage?

YOLO (You Only Look Once) treats detection as one regression problem: a single network pass divides the image into a grid and predicts boxes, confidence and class probabilities for every cell at once. That makes it very fast, suited to real-time video. Two-stage detectors are often more accurate on small or crowded objects but slower. YOLO has had many versions since the 2015 original, with anchors, multi-scale predictions and better backbones, so check the current release and licence before choosing one.
Also covers: grid cells, anchor boxes, Darknet, real-time detection.
A warehouse camera needs to count boxes on a conveyor in real time at 30 frames per second; a one-stage detector like YOLO is a natural fit.
What are IoU, non-maximum suppression and mAP?

Intersection over union (IoU) is the overlap area of the predicted and true boxes divided by their combined area; 1 is perfect, and a detection usually counts as correct above a threshold such as 0.5. Non-maximum suppression removes duplicate detections by keeping the highest-scoring box and discarding others that overlap it too much. Mean average precision (mAP) summarises detection quality: for each class compute average precision (the area under its precision-recall curve) at a chosen IoU threshold, then average across classes. COCO averages over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95.
Also covers: confidence threshold, precision-recall for detection.
A predicted box covers 8 units of area that overlap the true box in 6 units, with 10 units combined area: IoU = 0.6, so it counts as a hit at the 0.5 threshold.
What is semantic segmentation and what is U-Net?

Segmentation labels every pixel: semantic segmentation by class, instance segmentation by individual object. U-Net, built for biomedical images, is an encoder-decoder shaped like a U: a contracting path with convolutions and pooling captures context, an expanding path upsamples back to full size, and skip connections concatenate matching encoder features into the decoder to recover fine detail. It works well with small datasets and heavy augmentation, and remains a common backbone, including in diffusion models.
Also covers: fully convolutional networks, skip connections.
Given an MRI slice, U-Net outputs a mask that marks each pixel as tumour or not, giving the exact outline rather than just a yes or no.
What are Haar cascades and the Sobel filter?

A Haar cascade (Viola-Jones, 2001) detects objects such as faces quickly by computing simple rectangular contrast features on an integral image, picking the best with AdaBoost, and chaining classifiers in a cascade that rejects non-faces early. It is fast on a CPU but less accurate than modern deep detectors. The Sobel filter is a pair of 3 x 3 kernels that estimate the horizontal and vertical intensity gradient, so combining them highlights edges. Both are classic, hand-crafted techniques.
A hobbyist webcam project can use OpenCV's Haar cascade to find faces cheaply, while a production face detector would use a CNN-based model.
What are Pix2Pix and image-to-image translation?

Image-to-image translation converts one picture into another, such as sketches to photos, maps to satellite views or day to night. Pix2Pix is a conditional GAN trained on paired examples: the generator sees the input image and produces the output, the discriminator judges input and output together, and an added L1 loss keeps the output close to the target (the paper weights it heavily). CycleGAN handles unpaired data. Today diffusion-based editing is also common.
Training on pairs of building outlines and real facades teaches the model to turn a new outline sketch into a realistic-looking building.
What are vision transformers, CLIP and diffusion models?

Vision transformers split an image into patches and process them with transformer attention instead of convolutions; with enough data and pre-training they match or beat CNNs. CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together so matching image and caption embeddings are close, which enables zero-shot classification by comparing an image with text labels and powers many image search and generation systems. Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a gradual noising process, often guided by text. Check the current model landscape, it changes quickly.
Also covers: patch embeddings, contrastive learning, zero-shot.
To classify an image zero-shot, CLIP embeds the photo and the phrases 'a photo of a cat' and 'a photo of a dog', and picks the phrase whose embedding is closest.
How would you build a face recognition or attendance system, and what are the risks?

Detect faces, align and crop them, convert each into an embedding vector with a model trained for faces, and compare to stored embeddings by cosine distance with a threshold. Registration stores several embeddings per person; recognition finds the nearest match above the threshold, otherwise 'unknown'. Add liveness detection against photo spoofing, test across lighting, pose, glasses and skin tones, measure false accept and false reject rates, and log failures for review. Biometric data is sensitive: get explicit consent, minimise storage, secure it, follow local law (for example GDPR in the EU, or India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act; verify current requirements) and offer a non-biometric alternative.
Also covers: embeddings, verification vs identification, liveness, bias testing.
At an office entrance, the system compares a live face with 5,000 stored embeddings; a match score above 0.6 marks attendance. Photos held up to the camera are blocked by the liveness check.
What is NLP and what does a typical NLP pipeline look like?

Natural language processing is the field that lets computers read, interpret and generate human language. A classic pipeline: clean the text, tokenise, remove or keep stop words, normalise (lowercase, stemming or lemmatisation), convert to numbers (bag of words, TF-IDF or embeddings), then train a model for a task such as classification, tagging, translation or summarisation. Modern pipelines often skip most of the cleaning and fine-tune a pre-trained transformer directly. Common libraries: NLTK, spaCy, Gensim, TextBlob, scikit-learn and Hugging Face Transformers.
Also covers: libraries (NLTK, spaCy, Gensim, TextBlob, CoreNLP).
To flag angry customer emails: lowercase and tokenise, convert to TF-IDF, train logistic regression, or fine-tune a small transformer on 2,000 labelled emails for better accuracy.
What is tokenisation and why do modern models use subwords?

Tokenisation splits text into units called tokens: words, characters or pieces of words. Word-level tokens create huge vocabularies and cannot handle unseen words; characters make sequences very long. Subword methods such as byte-pair encoding, WordPiece and SentencePiece split rare words into frequent pieces, so any word can be represented with a vocabulary of tens of thousands. This is why language models can read new words and typos, and it also explains odd behaviour with numbers and spelling.
Also covers: BPE, WordPiece, vocabulary size.
The word 'unbelievably' might be split into 'un', 'believ', 'ably'. A model that never saw the whole word can still understand it from the parts.
What is the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?

Both reduce a word to a base form. Stemming chops suffixes using rules, quickly, and the result may not be a real word ('studies' becomes 'studi'). Lemmatisation uses vocabulary and grammar to return the dictionary form, the lemma ('better' becomes 'good', 'studies' becomes 'study'), which is more accurate but slower and needs the part of speech. For search and simple classifiers stemming may be enough; for meaning-sensitive tasks prefer lemmatisation.
Also covers: Porter stemmer, WordNet lemmatiser, stop words.
'running', 'runs' and 'ran' all map to the lemma 'run'. A stemmer might leave 'ran' unchanged because it only strips endings.
What are bag of words and n-grams?

Bag of words represents a document as counts of each vocabulary word, ignoring order, which gives a long, sparse vector that works well with linear models and Naive Bayes. N-grams extend it with sequences of n words (bigrams, trigrams) to keep a little context, such as 'not good'. The vocabulary grows quickly, so limit it with minimum frequency or maximum features. Embeddings and transformers capture meaning and order far better.
'It is going to rain today' becomes counts over the vocabulary [it, is, going, to, rain, today, ...] and 'not good' as a bigram stays distinct from 'good'.
What is TF-IDF and how is it calculated?

TF-IDF scores how important a word is to a document within a collection. Term frequency (TF) is how often the word appears in the document, often divided by the document length. Inverse document frequency (IDF) is the logarithm of the number of documents divided by the number containing the word, so rare words get a high weight and words in nearly every document score near zero. TF-IDF is TF multiplied by IDF. It is a strong baseline for search and classification, but it does not understand meaning.
Also covers: sparse vectors, cosine similarity for search, smoothing.
In a set of 1,000 news articles, 'the' appears everywhere and scores about zero, while 'tsunami' appears in 3 and scores high in those 3, which helps rank them for a tsunami search.
How does word2vec work (CBOW and skip-gram)?

Word2vec learns a dense vector for each word using a small neural network trained on a word-prediction task, so words used in similar contexts end up with similar vectors. CBOW predicts a word from its surrounding context words and is faster, good for frequent words and smaller data. Skip-gram predicts the surrounding words from a centre word and does better on rare words. Negative sampling makes training efficient. The vectors support analogies such as king - man + woman close to queen, though one vector per word cannot capture different senses.
Also covers: context window, embeddings, negative sampling.
From 'the cat sits on the mat', skip-gram with a window of 2 learns that 'sits' predicts 'cat' and 'on', so 'cat' and 'dog' end up close because they appear in similar contexts.
How are GloVe, fastText and doc2vec different from word2vec?

GloVe learns vectors from the global word co-occurrence counts of the whole corpus, so its vectors reflect global statistics, while word2vec streams over local windows; in practice they perform similarly. fastText represents a word as the sum of its character n-gram vectors, so it can build vectors for rare or unseen words and handles morphology. Doc2vec (paragraph vectors) extends word2vec to learn a vector for a whole paragraph or document. All give one fixed vector per token or document, unlike contextual models such as BERT.
A misspelling like 'recieve' has no word2vec vector, but fastText builds one from pieces like 'rec', 'eci', 'cie', which land near 'receive'.
How do you measure text similarity?

Lexical similarity compares the surface forms: edit distance (Levenshtein: the minimum insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another), Jaccard overlap of words, or TF-IDF with cosine similarity. Phonetic methods like Soundex match words that sound alike. Semantic similarity compares meaning by embedding the texts with sentence embeddings and taking cosine similarity. Word overlap can fail: 'the cat ate the mouse' and 'the mouse ate the cat food' overlap heavily but mean different things.
Also covers: Levenshtein distance, Soundex, cosine similarity, sentence embeddings.
The Levenshtein distance between HONDA and HYUNDAI is 3 (one substitution and two insertions). Soundex gives 'break' and 'brake' the same code, B620.
What are RNNs and why do they struggle with long sequences?

A recurrent neural network reads a sequence step by step and carries a hidden state that summarises what it has seen, applying the same weights at each step. Training uses backpropagation through time, and the gradient has to flow back through many steps, so it tends to vanish (early inputs are forgotten) or explode. This makes long-range dependencies hard to learn, and steps cannot be processed in parallel. LSTMs, GRUs and finally transformers address these problems.
Also covers: backpropagation through time, hidden state, gradient clipping.
In 'The keys that were on the table are missing', a plain RNN may forget that 'keys' is plural by the time it reaches 'are'.
How do LSTM and GRU work, and what are the gates?

An LSTM adds a memory cell and three gates, each a sigmoid that outputs numbers between 0 and 1 to control the flow: the forget gate decides what to erase from the cell, the input gate decides what new information to write, and the output gate decides what to expose as the hidden state. Because the cell state is updated mostly by addition, gradients flow over long spans. A GRU is a lighter version with two gates (update and reset) and no separate cell. Some notes list an 'activation gate' or 'hidden gate' as LSTM gates; those are not part of the standard design.
Also covers: cell state, gates, bidirectional RNNs.
When reading 'Maria was born in Spain... she speaks fluent ...', the LSTM's input gate stores 'Spain' and the forget gate keeps it alive over many words, so it can predict 'Spanish'.
What is the encoder-decoder (seq2seq) architecture?

An encoder reads the input sequence and compresses it into a representation; a decoder generates the output sequence from that representation one token at a time. It was first built with RNNs for machine translation, passing only a final fixed-size state, which loses information on long sentences. Attention fixed this by letting the decoder look back at all encoder states. Transformers keep the encoder-decoder idea in models such as T5, while many modern language models use only the decoder.
Also covers: bottleneck problem, attention, teacher forcing.
To translate English to French, the encoder reads 'How are you?' and the decoder writes 'Comment allez-vous ?' one word at a time, glancing at the English words as it goes.
What is attention and how does the transformer work?

Attention lets each token look at every other token and weigh how relevant each one is, building a context-aware representation. In self-attention each token produces a query, a key and a value; a token's query is compared with all keys, the scores are normalised with softmax, and the values are mixed by those weights. A transformer stacks layers of multi-head self-attention and feed-forward networks, with residual connections, layer normalisation and positional information, since attention itself has no sense of order. Because all positions are processed at once, training parallelises well on GPUs, which is why it replaced RNNs and scaled to today's large language models.
Also covers: Attention Is All You Need (2017), multi-head attention, positional encoding, quadratic cost in sequence length.
In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired', attention gives the word 'it' a high weight on 'animal', so the model resolves the pronoun.
How do BERT, GPT, ELMo, ULMFiT and XLNet differ?

ELMo (2018) produced contextual word vectors from a bidirectional LSTM language model. ULMFiT (2018) showed how to fine-tune a pre-trained LSTM language model for classification, using discriminative learning rates, slanted triangular schedules and gradual unfreezing. BERT (2018) is a transformer encoder pre-trained by masking words and predicting them, so it reads context in both directions and suits understanding tasks such as classification and question answering. GPT-style models are transformer decoders trained to predict the next token, so they generate text; scaled up, they became today's chat models. XLNet (2019) used a permutation-based objective to get bidirectional context while staying autoregressive.
Also covers: masked language modelling, autoregressive models, encoder-only vs decoder-only.
To classify support tickets, you might fine-tune BERT. To draft replies, you would prompt a GPT-style or other decoder-based chat model.
What are language models and perplexity?

A language model assigns probabilities to sequences of words, mostly by predicting the next token from the previous ones. N-gram models count short word sequences and suffer from sparsity; neural models learn much longer context. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts a held-out text: it is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token, so lower is better, and can be read as how many choices the model is effectively unsure between. Compare perplexities only for models using the same tokenisation and test text.
Also covers: n-gram models, data sparsity, applications (spelling, speech, translation).
A model with a perplexity of 20 on news text is as uncertain, on average, as if it were choosing among 20 equally likely words at each step.
What are named entity recognition and information extraction?

Named entity recognition finds and labels spans of text that name people, organisations, places, dates, amounts and so on. Information extraction goes further: it pulls structured facts from unstructured text, such as relations between entities and coreference (who 'she' refers to). Modern systems fine-tune transformers for token tagging, or use a large language model with a structured-output prompt, and are evaluated with precision, recall and F1 at the entity level. Related ideas: part-of-speech tagging, dependency and constituency parsing, which expose grammatical structure.
Also covers: dependency vs constituency parsing, pragmatics, coreference.
From 'Priya joined Infosys in Pune in March', NER marks Priya as PERSON, Infosys as ORG, Pune as LOCATION and March as DATE, which can then populate a database row.
What is topic modelling (LSA, pLSA, LDA, LDA2Vec)?

Topic modelling discovers themes in a collection of documents without labels. LSA/LSI factorises the term-document matrix with SVD to find latent concepts. pLSA models each document as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words, fitted with EM. LDA is the Bayesian version, putting Dirichlet priors on those distributions, which generalises better; it outputs, for each document, a mixture of topics, and for each topic, probable words. LDA2Vec combines LDA-style document topics with word2vec embeddings. Newer approaches, such as BERTopic, cluster transformer embeddings. You choose the number of topics and judge them by coherence and reading them.
Also covers: SVD, Dirichlet priors, EM algorithm, topic coherence.
Running LDA with 5 topics on 10,000 app reviews might reveal themes like 'login problems', 'pricing', 'battery drain', 'new features' and 'customer support', each shown as its top words.
How do sentiment analysis and text classification work?

Text classification assigns labels such as spam, topic or sentiment. Classic approach: TF-IDF features with logistic regression, Naive Bayes or SVM, which is a strong, cheap baseline. Better: fine-tune a pre-trained transformer, or prompt a large language model for zero-shot and few-shot labelling.
