For sentiment, polarity is how positive or negative the text is, and subjectivity is how opinionated versus factual; sarcasm, negation and domain slang make it hard. Evaluate with per-class precision, recall and F1, especially when classes are imbalanced.
Also covers: polarity, subjectivity, language detection, topic detection.
'The battery is fine, I guess, if you like waiting' is sarcastic; a bag-of-words model may call it positive, but a fine-tuned transformer is more likely to catch the sarcasm.
What is text summarisation, and how do extractive and abstractive differ?

Summarisation shortens a text while keeping the key points. Extractive methods select and stitch together the most important sentences from the original (using ranking such as TextRank), so they stay faithful but can read choppily. Abstractive methods generate new sentences, like a person would, using sequence-to-sequence or large language models; they read better but can hallucinate details. Evaluate with ROUGE for overlap, plus human or model-based checks for factual consistency.
Also covers: ROUGE, TextRank, faithfulness.

Summarising a 3-page contract extractively might pull out the clauses about payment and termination verbatim. An abstractive summary would write 'Either party may terminate with 30 days' notice', which needs checking against the text.
What are machine translation, text generation and word-sense disambiguation?

Neural machine translation maps text from one language to another with encoder-decoder or transformer models, evaluated with BLEU and increasingly with learned metrics. Text generation is language modelling used to produce new text one token at a time, with sampling settings such as temperature controlling randomness. Word-sense disambiguation chooses the right meaning of an ambiguous word from context: 'bank' in 'the bank will not accept cash' versus 'the river overflowed the bank'. Contextual embeddings solve much of this automatically.
Also covers: BLEU, temperature, beam search, WSD.
A translation system must decide whether 'bat' means the animal or the cricket equipment from the sentence. A contextual model reading 'He hit the ball with a bat' picks the equipment.
How do large language models, fine-tuning and RAG connect to classic NLP?

Large language models are transformers trained on huge text to predict the next token, then tuned to follow instructions. They have absorbed many classic NLP tasks, so classification, extraction, summarisation and translation can often be done by prompting. You can adapt them by fine-tuning, often with parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA that train a small set of added weights, and ground them in your documents with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) instead of retraining. Classic methods like TF-IDF, regex and small classifiers still win on cost, latency and control for narrow tasks. See the AI-PM Q&A for LLM design questions.
Also covers: prompting, LoRA, hallucination, when to use small models.

To tag 5 million product titles into 30 categories, a small fine-tuned classifier is much cheaper and faster than a large language model call per title. To answer customer questions from policy documents, RAG with an LLM fits better.
Walk through the forward pass and backpropagation of a simple neural network.

Forward pass: each layer computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, applies an activation function, and passes the result on until the output gives a prediction, from which the loss is computed. Backpropagation then applies the chain rule from the loss backwards: it computes how the loss changes with each layer's output, then with each weight and bias, reusing earlier results. An optimiser uses these gradients to update the weights. Automatic differentiation in PyTorch and TensorFlow does this for you.
Also covers: chain rule, computational graph, autograd.
For a single neuron y = w x + b with squared loss, the gradient with respect to w is the prediction error times x, so the update nudges w to shrink the error.
How do you choose a loss function?

Match the loss to the task and the noise: mean squared error for regression (sensitive to outliers); mean absolute error or Huber loss when outliers exist; binary cross-entropy for yes/no outputs; categorical cross-entropy for one-of-many classes; hinge loss for margin-based classifiers; focal loss to focus on hard examples in imbalanced detection; contrastive or triplet losses for learning similarity. The loss is what you optimise; the evaluation metric is what you report, and they can differ.
Also covers: Huber, focal loss, contrastive loss, label smoothing.
Predicting delivery time with a few extreme delays: Huber loss stops those outliers from dominating the training the way squared error would.
What is weight initialisation, and why does it matter?

Starting weights must break symmetry (not all equal) and keep the signal and gradients at a steady size across layers. If they are too small, signals vanish; too large, they explode. Xavier (Glorot) initialisation suits tanh or sigmoid layers; He initialisation suits ReLU layers. Frameworks pick sensible defaults, but they matter for very deep networks and custom layers.
Also covers: Xavier, He, symmetry breaking, zero initialisation.
Initialising every weight to zero makes all neurons in a layer learn exactly the same thing, so the layer behaves like a single neuron.
Compare SGD, momentum, RMSProp, Adam and AdamW.

Plain SGD steps along the gradient of a mini-batch. Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients to smooth the path and speed along consistent directions. RMSProp scales each parameter's step by a running average of its recent gradient size. Adam combines momentum and RMSProp-style scaling and is the common default. AdamW fixes how weight decay is applied (decoupled from the gradient update) and is widely used for transformers. SGD with momentum is still strong for many vision models.
Also covers: adaptive learning rates, weight decay, Nesterov momentum.
Training a transformer: AdamW with learning rate around 1e-4 to 3e-4 and weight decay about 0.01 to 0.1 is a common starting point (verify against the model's recipe).
How do learning-rate schedules and warmup work?

A fixed learning rate is rarely best. Schedules lower it over time (step decay, exponential, cosine annealing) so training makes big moves early and fine adjustments later. Warmup starts with a tiny rate and ramps up over the first steps, which stabilises Adam-style optimisers and large-batch or transformer training. Reduce-on-plateau cuts the rate when validation loss stalls. Finding a good peak learning rate is often the most valuable tuning step.
Also covers: cosine annealing, one-cycle, learning-rate finder.
A common transformer recipe: warm up linearly for the first few thousand steps, then decay with a cosine curve to a small value.
What are exploding gradients, and how do you fix them?

When gradients grow huge through many layers or time steps, weights jump wildly and the loss becomes NaN. Common in RNNs and very deep networks. Fixes: gradient clipping (cap the gradient norm), lower learning rate, better initialisation, normalisation layers, residual connections, and gated architectures such as LSTM. It is the counterpart of vanishing gradients.
Also covers: gradient clipping, NaN loss.
Training suddenly shows loss = NaN after a few hundred steps; adding gradient-norm clipping at 1.0 and lowering the learning rate stops it.
What do batch normalisation and layer normalisation do, and when do you use each?

Normalisation layers rescale activations to a stable range, which speeds up and steadies training. Batch normalisation normalises each feature over the mini-batch; it works well in CNNs but depends on batch size and behaves differently at training and inference time. Layer normalisation normalises across the features of each individual example, so it does not depend on batch size and is the standard in transformers and RNNs. RMSNorm is a simpler variant common in recent large language models.
Also covers: group norm, RMSNorm, running statistics, pre-norm vs post-norm.
With tiny batches (such as 2 images per GPU), batch norm statistics become noisy, so group norm or layer norm is often preferred.
Why do residual (skip) connections help very deep networks?

A residual block outputs the input plus a learned change: y = x + F(x). The identity path gives gradients a direct route backwards, which eases vanishing gradients, and makes it easy for a layer to learn 'do nothing' if that is best. This is what allowed ResNets with hundreds of layers and is built into every transformer block.
Also covers: identity shortcut, degradation problem.
Without skip connections, a 56-layer plain CNN trained worse than a 20-layer one in the original ResNet study; with them, deeper became better.
Which regularisation techniques work for neural networks?

Weight decay (L2), dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, label smoothing, normalisation layers, smaller models, and more data. Also noise injection, stochastic depth and mixup. Choose by watching the gap between training and validation loss: a widening gap means more regularisation or more data; both losses high means a bigger model or longer training.
Also covers: early stopping, mixup, stochastic depth, label smoothing.
An image classifier with 99% training but 85% validation accuracy improves after adding random crops, flips and dropout before the classifier head.
What is the universal approximation theorem, and what does it not promise?

It says a network with one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any reasonable continuous function on a bounded range. It does not say how many neurons you need, that training will find the right weights, or that the result will generalise. In practice depth, good architectures and lots of data matter more than the existence result.
A one-hidden-layer network can in theory fit a complicated curve, but a very wide one may be impractical to train compared with a deeper, narrower one.
Which activation functions are used today, and why?

ReLU is the simple default (zero for negatives, identity for positives) and fixes much of the vanishing gradient problem, but neurons can 'die'. Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope for negatives. GELU, a smooth version, is common in transformers like BERT and GPT-style models. SwiGLU, a gated variant, appears in many recent large language models. Sigmoid and tanh remain in gates and output layers; softmax for multi-class outputs.
Also covers: Leaky ReLU, GELU, SiLU, SwiGLU, dying ReLU.
A feed-forward block in a modern language model often uses SwiGLU instead of ReLU because it tends to give better quality at the same size (verify for the specific model).
What do overparameterisation, double descent and grokking tell us about generalisation?

Classical theory said very large models must overfit. In practice, huge networks that fit the training data perfectly can still generalise, and test error can fall again after the point where the model first interpolates the data (double descent). Grokking is a case where a network suddenly generalises long after fitting the training set. The explanations (implicit regularisation by SGD, simple solutions being found first) are still being researched, so treat them as active research and not settled rules.
Also covers: interpolation threshold, implicit regularisation.
Making a model larger can first increase test error and then reduce it again, which is why 'just use a smaller model' is not always the right fix.
How do you debug a neural network that is not learning?

Start simple: check the data and labels (look at samples), confirm shapes, and try to overfit a tiny batch of 10 examples; if that fails there is a bug. Then check the loss starts near the expected value (about log of the number of classes for a classifier), try a learning-rate sweep, check normalisation of inputs, make sure train and eval modes are right, look for NaNs, and inspect gradients and activation statistics. Change one thing at a time and track experiments.
Also covers: overfit a single batch, sanity checks, learning-rate sweep.
A 10-class classifier whose loss sits at 2.30 forever (about the natural log of 10) is guessing; the cause might be a frozen layer, a learning rate that is far too small, or mismatched labels.
What is model calibration, and how do you fix a miscalibrated model?

A model is calibrated if, among predictions it labels 80% likely, about 80% really are positive. Modern neural networks are often overconfident. Check with reliability diagrams and expected calibration error. Fixes after training: temperature scaling, Platt scaling, or isotonic regression on a validation set. Calibration matters when probabilities drive decisions such as pricing, risk, or deciding when to defer to a human.
Also covers: reliability diagram, temperature scaling, Platt scaling.
A fraud model that says 99% on cases that are only fraudulent 70% of the time will cause too many blocked customers if thresholds assume the stated probabilities.
How do you train efficiently at scale: mixed precision, gradient accumulation and distributed training?

Mixed precision does most maths in 16-bit (FP16 or BF16) for speed and memory, keeping critical values in 32-bit. Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several small batches before one update, simulating a large batch on limited memory. Data parallelism copies the model to several GPUs, each processing part of the batch; model, pipeline, and tensor parallelism split the model itself when it does not fit on one device; sharding methods such as ZeRO or FSDP split optimiser states and weights.
Also covers: BF16, FSDP, ZeRO, tensor parallelism.
To train with an effective batch of 256 on a GPU that fits 32, accumulate gradients over 8 steps before each update.
Explain self-attention step by step, including queries, keys, values and the square-root scaling.

Each token's vector is turned into three vectors by learned matrices: a query (what am I looking for), a key (what do I contain) and a value (what I will pass on). A token's attention scores are the dot products of its query with every key; dividing by the square root of the key dimension stops the scores growing with dimension and saturating the softmax; softmax turns them into weights that sum to 1; the output is the weighted sum of the value vectors. Every token can look at every other token in one step.
Also covers: scaled dot-product attention, attention weights, softmax.
In 'The bank raised rates', the token 'bank' puts high weight on 'raised' and 'rates', so its new vector reflects the finance sense, not the river sense.
What is multi-head attention, and why use several heads?

Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each with its own query, key and value projections on a smaller dimension, then concatenates and mixes the results. Different heads can specialise in different relationships, such as syntax, nearby words, or long-range references. Interpretability studies suggest heads do specialise, but not every head is equally useful, and some can be pruned.
Also covers: head dimension, concatenation, output projection.
One head might track which noun a pronoun refers to, while another focuses on the previous word.
How does a transformer know word order? Compare sinusoidal, learned, RoPE and ALiBi positions.

Self-attention alone ignores order, so position information is added. The original transformer used fixed sinusoidal encodings added to the embeddings; BERT-style models learn position embeddings. Many recent large language models use rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which rotate queries and keys by position-dependent angles so attention depends on relative distance. ALiBi adds a distance penalty directly to attention scores. Methods differ in how well they extend to longer inputs than seen in training, which is an active area.
Also covers: relative position, context extension.
Without any positional signal, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look identical to the attention layer.
What is the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder transformers?

Encoder-only models (BERT-style) see the whole input in both directions and suit understanding tasks: classification, tagging, search embeddings. Decoder-only models (GPT-style) read left to right with a causal mask and generate text one token at a time; they power most current chat models. Encoder-decoder models (T5, original transformer) encode the input, then generate output while attending to it; strong for translation and summarisation. Most frontier language models today are decoder-only.
Also covers: causal mask, cross-attention, BERT, GPT, T5.
For finding similar support tickets use an encoder embedding model; for drafting a reply use a decoder-only chat model.
What is causal masking, and what are the pre-training objectives of BERT and GPT?

A causal mask stops each position from attending to later positions, so when predicting the next token the model cannot peek at the answer. GPT-style models train on next-token prediction (causal language modelling). BERT trains on masked language modelling, predicting randomly hidden words from both sides, originally plus a next-sentence task that later work found of little value. The objective shapes what the model is good at: generation versus understanding.
Also covers: masked language modelling, next-token prediction, teacher forcing.
Given 'The cat sat on the ___', a GPT model predicts the next word using only the left context; BERT could also use words to the right if the blank is in the middle.
What is a KV cache, and why does LLM inference depend on it?

When a decoder generates token by token, the keys and values of earlier tokens do not change, so the model stores them (the KV cache) and only computes the new token's query, key and value. This saves a lot of computation but uses memory that grows with sequence length, batch size and layers, which often limits how many users a GPU can serve. Techniques such as grouped-query attention and paged caching reduce the cost.
Also covers: paged attention, memory bandwidth, prefill vs decode.
A long chat with a big model can fill GPU memory with cache before computation becomes the bottleneck, so serving cost depends on conversation length.
What are FlashAttention, multi-query and grouped-query attention?

Standard attention builds a large sequence-by-sequence score matrix, which is slow and memory hungry. FlashAttention computes the same exact result in small tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory, cutting memory traffic and making long contexts practical. Multi-query attention (MQA) shares one set of keys and values across all heads, and grouped-query attention (GQA) shares them across groups of heads; both shrink the KV cache and speed up inference with small quality loss.
Also covers: IO-aware algorithms, memory bandwidth.
A model switching from full multi-head to grouped-query attention can serve more concurrent users on the same GPU because its cache is several times smaller.
What is a mixture of experts (MoE) model?

A mixture-of-experts layer replaces one large feed-forward block with many smaller expert blocks plus a router that sends each token to only a few of them. The model has a very large total number of parameters but uses just a fraction per token, giving more capacity at similar compute. Challenges: balancing load across experts, training stability, and needing memory for all experts. Several recent large models are reported to use MoE; details of specific commercial models are often not public.
Also covers: router, sparse activation, load balancing.
A model with 100 billion total parameters that activates 15 billion per token can answer with the compute of a 15-billion model while storing more knowledge.
How does tokenisation work (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece), and why does it matter?

Models read tokens, not words. Byte-pair encoding starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent pairs into larger pieces; WordPiece and SentencePiece are related methods (SentencePiece also works directly on raw text, including spaces). Tokenisation affects cost (you pay per token), context limits, handling of rare words, numbers, code and non-English languages, and can explain odd model behaviour such as trouble with counting letters.
Also covers: vocabulary size, byte-level, out-of-vocabulary words.
A word like 'unhappiness' might become 'un', 'happiness' or three smaller pieces; text in some languages can take several times more tokens than English for the same meaning.
What are scaling laws, and what did the Chinchilla result say?

Scaling laws are empirical findings that model loss falls smoothly and predictably as you increase parameters, data and compute. The Chinchilla study (DeepMind, 2022) argued that for a fixed compute budget, many large models were under-trained: parameters and training tokens should grow roughly in proportion, on the order of 20 tokens per parameter. Later practice often trains smaller models on far more data because inference cost matters too, so treat the exact ratio as guidance, not a law.
Also covers: compute-optimal training, over-training, emergent abilities debate.
A team with a fixed budget gets a better model by training a 7B model on 1.4 trillion tokens than a 20B model on far fewer, under this logic (verify the numbers in the paper before quoting).
How do pre-training, fine-tuning, instruction tuning and RLHF or DPO differ?

Pre-training learns language from huge unlabelled text by predicting tokens. Supervised fine-tuning on examples of instructions and good answers makes the model follow requests (instruction tuning). Preference tuning then aligns it with human judgements: RLHF trains a reward model from human rankings and optimises the language model against it with reinforcement learning (often PPO); DPO reaches a similar goal directly from preference pairs without a separate reward model. Newer methods also use verifiable rewards for reasoning tasks.
Also covers: reward model, PPO, DPO, RLAIF.
A base model asked 'How do I bake bread?' may continue with another question; after instruction tuning and preference tuning it gives a helpful, safe step-by-step answer.
What are LoRA and QLoRA, and when do you use parameter-efficient fine-tuning?

Full fine-tuning updates all weights, which is expensive. LoRA freezes the original weights and learns small low-rank update matrices added to selected layers, training a tiny fraction of parameters. QLoRA does this on top of a base model quantised to 4-bit, so large models can be tuned on one GPU. You get small adapter files that can be swapped per task. Use it when you have limited data or compute; full fine-tuning can still win when you have lots of data and need maximum change.
Also covers: adapters, low-rank, rank r, PEFT.
A company keeps one base model and ships separate small LoRA adapters for legal, support and finance tasks, loading the right one per request.
What are hallucinations in language models, and how do you reduce them?

Hallucinations are fluent but false or unsupported outputs, because the model predicts plausible text, not verified facts. Reduce them with retrieval-augmented generation grounded in trusted documents, asking for citations and checking them, constraining outputs (structured formats, tool use for calculations and lookups), better prompts that allow 'I don't know', fine-tuning on high-quality data, evaluation sets that measure factuality, and human review for high-stakes use. They cannot be eliminated entirely.
Also covers: grounding, retrieval, citations, factuality evaluation.
An assistant asked about a regulation should quote the retrieved paragraph and its source; if nothing relevant is retrieved it should say so, not invent a clause.
How does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) work, and how do embeddings and vector search fit in?

Split documents into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding vector with an embedding model, and store them in a vector index. For a question, embed it, retrieve the nearest chunks (often combined with keyword search and a re-ranker), put them into the prompt, and have the language model answer using them. Quality depends on chunking, embedding choice, retrieval and re-ranking, prompt design and evaluation. See the AI-PM Q&A for system-level depth.
Also covers: cosine similarity, hybrid search, re-ranking, chunking.
A support bot retrieves the three help-centre paragraphs closest to 'How do I reset my password?' and answers only from those.
How do Vision Transformers and CLIP work?

A Vision Transformer (ViT) splits an image into fixed patches, turns each patch into a vector, adds position information, and runs a standard transformer over the sequence; with enough data it matches or beats CNNs. CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together so that matching image-caption pairs land close in a shared space (contrastive learning), enabling zero-shot classification by comparing an image with text labels. Many multimodal models build on these ideas.
Also covers: patch embedding, contrastive learning, zero-shot, multimodal models.
To classify a photo with CLIP, embed the image and the phrases 'a photo of a cat' and 'a photo of a dog', then pick the phrase with the closest embedding.
How do diffusion models generate images?

Diffusion models learn to reverse a noising process. In training, noise is added to images step by step and a network learns to predict and remove that noise. To generate, start from pure noise and repeatedly denoise, guided by a text embedding, until an image appears. Latent diffusion does this in a compressed space for speed. Compared with GANs, diffusion is usually more stable to train but slower to sample, which faster samplers and distillation try to fix.
Also covers: denoising, classifier-free guidance, latent diffusion, GANs.
A prompt such as 'a red bicycle on a beach' steers each denoising step so the random noise gradually turns into a picture matching the text.
What are state space models and Mamba, and do they replace transformers?

State space models process a sequence with a compact running state, so their cost grows linearly with length instead of quadratically as in full attention. Mamba added input-dependent (selective) state updates and showed strong results on language and other sequences. They are promising for very long inputs, and some recent models mix attention and state-space layers. As of my knowledge they have not clearly replaced transformers at the frontier, and this area changes quickly, so check recent results.
Also covers: linear-time sequence models, hybrid architectures.
For streaming sensor data with millions of steps, a state space model may be far cheaper than attention over the whole history.
How are large language models evaluated, and what are the pitfalls?

Use several layers: automatic benchmarks (knowledge, reasoning, code), task-specific test sets built from your own data, model-graded evaluation (using a strong model as judge, which has its own biases), and human review or pairwise preference comparisons. Pitfalls: benchmark contamination (test data seen in training), overfitting to leaderboards, judge bias toward long or confident answers, and metrics that do not match user value. Always measure on your use case.
Also covers: contamination, LLM-as-judge, pairwise comparison, evals.
A model scores highly on a public quiz benchmark but fails your company's contract questions; a 200-question test built from real contracts reveals this.
What is quantisation, and how is it used for LLM inference?

Quantisation stores weights (and sometimes activations or the KV cache) with fewer bits, such as 8-bit or 4-bit instead of 16-bit, cutting memory and often speeding inference with a small accuracy loss. Methods include post-training approaches such as GPTQ and AWQ, and quantisation-aware training. Always test quality on your tasks, since some capabilities degrade more than average scores suggest.
Also covers: INT8, INT4, GPTQ, AWQ.
Going from 16-bit to 4-bit shrinks a 70-billion-parameter model from roughly 140 GB to roughly 35 GB of weights, which can fit on far fewer GPUs.
What is speculative decoding?

A small, fast draft model proposes several next tokens, and the large model checks them all in one pass, accepting those that match what it would have produced and correcting the first mismatch. Output quality is the same as with the large model alone, but latency drops when the draft is often right.
A 1B draft model guesses the next 5 tokens of a common phrase; the 70B model verifies them in one step instead of five.
What are reasoning models and chain-of-thought, and what is test-time compute?

Chain-of-thought prompting asks a model to show intermediate steps, which often improves multi-step problems. Reasoning models are trained, often with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks like maths and code, to produce long internal reasoning before answering. Test-time compute means spending more computation at answer time (longer thinking, sampling several attempts and voting) to improve quality, at higher cost and latency. This area is developing fast, so check current documentation for specific models.
Also covers: self-consistency, verifiable rewards, thinking budget.
For a tricky logic puzzle, letting the model think step by step or sample five answers and take the majority usually beats a single quick answer, but costs more.
How do you handle long context, and what are its limits?

Options: models trained or adapted for longer windows (position-encoding extensions), efficient attention and caching, summarising or chunking, and retrieval to pick only relevant parts. Limits: cost and latency grow with length, and models can miss details in the middle of very long inputs ('lost in the middle'), so a bigger window does not guarantee better use of it. Test recall on your own long documents.
Also covers: lost in the middle, needle-in-a-haystack tests, retrieval vs long context.
Pasting a 300-page contract works only if the model reliably finds the clause you ask about; a needle test with planted facts shows whether it does.
What are the main safety and responsible-AI concerns for modern models, and what do you do about them?

Concerns: hallucination, bias and unfair outcomes, privacy leakage and memorised training data, prompt injection and misuse, copyright and data provenance, over-reliance, and environmental cost. Practices: documented data sources, red-teaming and safety evaluations, guardrails and content filters, access controls, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, monitoring after launch, and following the laws and standards that apply to you (rules differ by region and change, so check current requirements).
Also covers: red-teaming, prompt injection, model cards, guardrails.
Before launching a loan-assistant bot, test it on adversarial prompts, check subgroup performance, restrict what data it can access, and keep a human approver for rejections.
How do Python, R, SQL and SAS compare for data science?

Python is the general-purpose default: a huge ecosystem (pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch), easy to take from analysis to production. R is strong for statistics, visualisation and academic work. SQL is not optional: most data lives in databases, and you use it to pull, join and aggregate data before modelling. SAS is a commercial tool still common in banking, insurance and pharma, with strong governance and support but licence costs. Most teams use SQL plus Python, and pick R or SAS where the industry expects it.
Also covers: open source vs commercial, when to use each.
A churn project pulls two years of orders with SQL, builds features and models in Python, and the risk team's validation report is produced in SAS because the regulator expects it.
Which Python libraries should a data scientist know, and what does each do?

NumPy for fast arrays and maths; pandas for tables (read, clean, group, join, reshape); matplotlib and seaborn (or plotly) for charts; SciPy and statsmodels for statistics and tests; scikit-learn for classical models, preprocessing, pipelines and metrics; XGBoost, LightGBM or CatBoost for boosting; PyTorch or TensorFlow/Keras for deep learning; Hugging Face Transformers for pre-trained language and vision models; spaCy and NLTK for text. Learn to read the documentation, since APIs change between versions; if unsure whether a function exists, check the current docs.
Also covers: joblib, imbalanced-learn, Gensim, OpenCV.
A typical notebook: pandas loads a CSV, seaborn plots distributions, a scikit-learn pipeline imputes, scales and fits a model, cross_val_score reports the metric, and joblib saves the pipeline.
TensorFlow, Keras, PyTorch or JAX: how do you choose?

PyTorch is the most common in research and increasingly in production, with a flexible, Pythonic style and a large ecosystem (including Hugging Face). TensorFlow, with Keras as its high-level API, has strong deployment tooling (TF Serving, TF Lite) and remains widely used in industry. Keras 3 can run on multiple backends including TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch (verify current status). JAX is favoured for high-performance research. Older notes mention Theano, which is no longer developed, and TensorFlow 1.x static graphs; TensorFlow 2 uses eager execution by default. I choose what the team and the model ecosystem support.
Also covers: Theano is discontinued, eager vs graph, TF Lite, ONNX.
To fine-tune a pre-trained language model from Hugging Face you will almost certainly write PyTorch. To ship a small model to an Android phone, TF Lite or ONNX conversion may be your route.
What are tensors, and what do TensorBoard and experiment trackers do?

In deep learning a tensor is a multi-dimensional array of numbers, the data structure that frameworks use for inputs, weights and outputs, with a shape such as (batch, height, width, channels), plus support for automatic differentiation and GPUs. TensorBoard visualises training: loss and metric curves, model graphs, histograms and embeddings. Tools such as MLflow and Weights and Biases track experiments, parameters, metrics and artefacts so runs are comparable and reproducible.
Also covers: shapes, autograd, GPU tensors.
A batch of 32 colour images of 224 x 224 pixels is one tensor of shape (32, 3, 224, 224) in PyTorch. TensorBoard shows whether validation loss starts rising, a sign of overfitting.
How do Hadoop, Spark and PySpark fit into data science work?

Hadoop (HDFS plus MapReduce) pioneered storing and processing data across many machines; it is now mostly legacy, replaced by cloud storage and warehouses. Spark processes large data in memory across a cluster and is the standard for big-data transformation and machine learning at scale; PySpark is its Python API. Spark uses lazy evaluation (transformations build a plan; actions such as count run it), partitions data, and shuffles are expensive. Use it when data does not fit on one machine; otherwise pandas, DuckDB or SQL are simpler.
Also covers: Cloudera/CDH, distributed computing, partitions, shuffle.
Aggregating 2 billion clickstream rows by user in a nightly job suits Spark. Analysing a 2 GB file on a laptop is faster to do in pandas or DuckDB.
How do you write good SQL for data science, and what does an interview test?

Interviews usually test joins, GROUP BY with aggregates, HAVING, subqueries and CTEs, window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, running totals), handling NULLs and dates, and de-duplication. Habits: filter early, know the grain of each table, check join keys for duplicates before aggregating, and sanity-check row counts. Common tasks: top N per group, month-over-month change, retention and funnel counts, and second-highest salary. Dialects differ slightly, so check the syntax of the database you use.
Also covers: CTE, window functions, self-joins, anti-joins.
'Find each customer's most recent order' is done with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) and keeping row number 1.
How do you make data science work reproducible and shareable?

Fix random seeds, pin library versions (requirements file or lock file) or use a Docker image, keep code in version control, version data and models (tools such as DVC or MLflow can help), track every experiment with its parameters and metrics, write preprocessing as code, and separate exploration notebooks from tested pipeline code. A teammate should be able to rebuild any reported number from a commit and a dataset version.
A stakeholder asks 'why did the score change since last month?' With versioned data and logged runs, you can show that the training window moved and a feature definition changed.
How do you use GPUs and cloud notebooks efficiently for training?

Deep learning needs GPUs (or TPUs) for matrix maths; free or low-cost notebook services such as Google Colab are fine for learning and prototypes, cloud instances for real training. Tips: develop and debug on a tiny subset, measure data-loading time so the GPU is not idle, use mixed precision and larger batches where memory allows, checkpoint often so a lost session does not waste a run, and shut instances down when done. For multiple GPUs, data parallelism splits each batch across them.
Debugging on 1% of the data takes minutes on a CPU. Only after the loss curve looks right do you launch the full multi-hour run on a GPU instance.
How do you deploy a machine learning model?

First decide the pattern: batch scoring on a schedule, real-time prediction through an API, streaming, or on-device (edge). Save the whole pipeline (preprocessing plus model), wrap it in a service such as FastAPI or Flask with input validation, package it with its dependencies in a Docker container, and deploy it to cloud or on-premise infrastructure depending on the client's constraints, behind a load balancer with health checks. Release gradually with canary or shadow deployments, and keep a rollback. Set latency and availability targets (SLA) up front.
Also covers: cloud vs on-premise, edge deployment, API, SLA.
A fraud model is wrapped in an API that answers in under 100 ms, runs as five container copies, and first receives 5% of live traffic. If metrics hold for a week, it goes to 100%.
What should you log and monitor for a model in production?

Log requests, inputs (or features), predictions, model version, latency and errors, plus later-arriving true outcomes. Monitor system health (uptime, latency, error rate, resource use), data quality (missing values, schema changes), data drift (input distribution shifts), prediction drift, and model quality once labels arrive, plus business metrics. Alert on thresholds, with fatal errors paged or emailed and warnings in a dashboard. Store logs somewhere queryable (a database or log platform) so failures can be investigated.
Also covers: logging, alerting, dashboards, MongoDB or other log stores.
A scoring service logs each request with an ID and model version. An alert fires when the share of missing 'income' values jumps from 2% to 40%, pointing to an upstream data bug.
What are data drift and concept drift, and how often should you retrain?

Data drift is a change in the input distribution (new customer mix); concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the target (customer behaviour changes). Detect them by comparing live and training distributions with measures such as the population stability index or Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, and by tracking accuracy when labels arrive. Rather than a fixed calendar (some study notes say 'every 20 days'), I prefer triggers: retrain when drift or quality passes a threshold, with a regular schedule as a backstop sized to how fast the domain changes and how long labels take to arrive.
Also covers: PSI, KS test, retraining triggers, champion-challenger.
A demand model degrades when a competitor opens nearby. The error alert triggers retraining on the last 8 weeks, and the new model runs in shadow mode for a week before replacing the old one.
How do you handle model failures and keep improving the model?

Capture the cases where the model was wrong or unsure: store the input, prediction and confidence, send a regular summary to the support or data team, and route low-confidence cases to a human. Review them for patterns (lighting, a new product, a data bug), label them, add them to the training set, and retrain, then test the new model on a fixed set of past failures to confirm they are fixed without breaking other cases. This human-in-the-loop cycle turns production mistakes into training data.
Also covers: human-in-the-loop, error analysis, hard-example mining.
A face-recognition system stores every failed match. Each week a reviewer labels the 200 worst, and the retrained model fixes most of the low-light failures.
How do you automate data pipelines and scheduling, and validate data in them?

Build extract, transform and load (ETL or ELT) steps as code, with a scheduler or orchestrator such as cron, Airflow or a cloud workflow service to run them on time, retry, and alert on failure. Add data validation at the edges: schema checks, ranges, null rates, row counts and freshness (libraries such as Great Expectations can help; verify current features). Make steps idempotent so re-running is safe. Retraining jobs can be scheduled the same way.
Also covers: ETL, Airflow, idempotency, schema checks.

A nightly pipeline loads yesterday's orders, checks that row counts are within 20% of the weekly average, builds features, and writes them to a table. If the count check fails, the job stops and pages the owner.
What is the difference between dev, UAT and production environments, and how does CI/CD apply to ML?

Development is where you build and experiment; UAT (user acceptance testing) or staging mirrors production so users and testers can verify behaviour; production serves real users. Continuous integration runs tests on every change (code, data checks, a model quality gate); continuous delivery promotes the packaged artefact from one environment to the next. For ML add a model registry with versions, reproducible training, automated evaluation against a fixed test set, and gradual rollout. Train once, then promote the same artefact through environments, as the source notes do.
Also covers: model registry, quality gates, rollback.
A new model passes unit tests and beats the current one on a fixed 2,000-case benchmark, is registered as version 14, deployed to UAT for business checks, then rolled out to production in stages.
How long does training take, and how do you scale it?

It depends on data size, model size, batch size, number of epochs and hardware, so estimate by timing a small run and extrapolating, and report hardware with the number. To scale: use a faster or multiple GPUs (data parallelism), larger batches with a tuned learning rate, mixed precision, efficient data loading, transfer learning to cut epochs, early stopping, and checkpoints. Be wary of quoted figures out of context: a published 'model trained for 110 hours' says nothing about your problem.
Also covers: data parallelism, mixed precision, checkpointing.
Timing 100 steps at batch size 64 at 0.5 seconds each means one epoch of 100,000 images takes about 13 minutes; 30 epochs is about 6.5 hours.
How do you make a model small and fast enough for edge or low-cost serving?

Options: quantisation (store weights in 8-bit or lower), pruning (remove unimportant weights), knowledge distillation (train a small student to imitate a large teacher), efficient architectures (MobileNet-style models), and compilation or runtime tools such as ONNX Runtime or TF Lite. Measure accuracy loss against latency, size and cost, and test on the target device. See the AI-PM Q&A for the LLM-specific versions.
Also covers: distillation, quantisation, edge devices such as Google Coral.
A phone app needs a face detector under 20 ms and 10 MB. Quantising a MobileNet-style model to 8-bit meets the size and speed target with a small accuracy drop.
How do you address bias, fairness and privacy in data science work?

Check how the data was collected and who is missing; measure performance by subgroup (not just overall) and compare error rates; examine features that proxy for protected attributes; and choose fairness definitions with stakeholders because they can conflict. Mitigate with better data, reweighting, threshold adjustments, or constraints, then monitor after launch. Language models trained on human text can pick up gender and other biases, shown in studies of word embeddings and coreference. For privacy: minimise and anonymise data, secure access, honour consent and retention rules, and consider techniques such as differential privacy. Legal requirements vary by country, so check them.
Also covers: gender bias in NLP, subgroup metrics, proxies, differential privacy.
A hiring-screen model that scores resumes lower for women's college names is a proxy problem. Auditing selection rates by group exposes it, and removing proxy features plus re-testing helps.
Can NLP on news headlines predict stock-market movements?

It can find weak signals, such as sentiment toward a company, but it is much harder than it looks. News is quickly priced in, markets are noisy, and the classic mistakes are look-ahead leakage (using information from after the trade time), overfitting to a short history, ignoring costs, and mistaking correlation for a tradable edge. A sound approach uses strict time-based validation, realistic backtests with transaction costs, and a sceptical attitude to any impressive result. This is a modelling discussion, not financial advice.
A model that scores headline sentiment shows a 0.2 correlation with next-day returns in-sample, which vanishes once it is tested on later months with fees included.
Tell me about your most recent data science project.

Use a simple structure: the business problem and why it mattered, the data (source, size, quality), your approach and why you chose it, the result in numbers, how it was deployed and used, and what you learned. Keep it to about two minutes, use your own real project, and make your own contribution clear. If you lack a work project, present a portfolio or competition project honestly as such. The study notes give a scripted face-attendance example; do not copy someone else's numbers.
Also covers: STAR or problem-approach-result structure, honesty about your role.

'Our customers cancelled at 18% a year. I built a gradient-boosting model on 24 months of usage data, caught 55% of cancellers with 30% precision, and the retention team's calls cut churn in the pilot group from 18% to 15%.'
What was the size and type of your data, and how did you check its quality?

State rows, columns, time span, storage and the kind: tabular, text, images, time series, structured or unstructured. Then explain the quality checks: schema and types, duplicates, missing and impossible values, class balance, label quality, representativeness (does it cover the conditions the model will meet?), and drift between training and live data. Mention how images or text were converted into tensors, if relevant. Real figures matter: interviewers probe for consistency.
Also covers: data validation, enrichment, labelling quality.
'About 2.3 million orders over 3 years, 40 columns, 1.8% fraud. Three percent had missing postcodes; I checked that missingness was not concentrated in fraud cases before imputing.'
How big was your team and what was your role in it?

Name the roles around you (product manager, data engineers, data scientists, ML engineers, QA, designers, DevOps) and exactly what you owned: scoping, data, modelling, evaluation, deployment, stakeholder communication. Interviewers want to know how you collaborate, so mention a disagreement you helped resolve or a handover you managed. Claim only what you did.
Also covers: roles and responsibilities, day-to-day tasks, scrum, UAT support.

'A team of eight: a product manager, two data engineers, three data scientists, a QA engineer and a DevOps engineer. I owned feature design and evaluation, and wrote the acceptance criteria with the product manager.'
Which part of the project did you contribute to most?

Pick one area where you drove an outcome and can go deep, such as problem framing, a feature set that lifted the metric, an evaluation design that caught leakage, or a deployment fix, and be ready for follow-up questions on any detail. Link it to a result. Do not list everything; depth is more convincing than breadth.

'I found our validation set shared customers with training. Re-splitting by customer dropped the offline score from 0.93 to 0.84, which matched what we saw live, so we avoided shipping a model that would have disappointed.'
What were the biggest challenges, and how did you handle them?

Typical real challenges: getting enough clean, labelled data; labelling effort; choosing between algorithms; model performance on rare cases; meeting the API's latency target; and changing requirements. Describe one or two honestly, what you tried, what worked, and what you would do differently. Showing judgement is more valuable than a flawless story.
Also covers: data availability, labelling cost, SLA, stakeholder alignment.

'Only 600 labelled defects existed. We used augmentation and a pre-trained backbone, and set up an active-learning loop where inspectors labelled the 50 most uncertain images a week. Recall rose from 62% to 81% in six weeks.'
How did you validate and enrich your data?

Validation: check the data covers real conditions (for images: lighting, distance, angles, alignment; for tabular data: segments, seasons), check labels on a sample, and look for duplicates and leakage. Enrichment: for vision, augmentation such as flips, crops, brightness and colour changes; for tabular and text data, adding derived features, external data, or more diverse examples. Always evaluate on untouched, unaugmented data.
'Photos from only daytime were over-represented, so I added brightness and contrast augmentation and collected 300 evening photos. Night-time accuracy rose from 71% to 86%.'
What data preprocessing steps did you apply?

Describe the steps you actually used and why: de-duplicating, fixing types, handling missing values (impute, flag or drop), outliers, encoding categoricals (dropping one dummy to avoid the dummy-variable trap), scaling for distance- or gradient-based models, creating features, dimensionality reduction when features were many, and for deep learning, resizing, normalising and augmenting images. State that every step was fitted on training data only and wrapped in a pipeline.
Also covers: cleaning, integration, scaling, encoding, PCA.
'I dropped an ID column, filled missing ages with the median plus a flag, one-hot encoded the city, standardised income and fitted all of it inside a pipeline so cross-validation stayed leak-free.'
How did you improve or optimise your model?

Show a method rather than a list of tricks: set a baseline, do error analysis to see what fails, then improve in order of impact: better data (quality and quantity), better features, a more suitable model, hyperparameter tuning with cross-validation, regularization against overfitting, learning-rate schedules, ensembling, and finally threshold tuning for the business cost. For a neural network also: transfer learning, tuning batch size and learning rate, and using softmax (not sigmoid) for multi-class outputs. Report how much each change helped.
Also covers: error analysis, tuning, ensembling, schedule, reduce-on-plateau.
'Baseline AUC 0.78. Fixing label noise: 0.80. Adding recency features: 0.84. Switching to gradient boosting: 0.87. Tuning and ensembling added 0.005, so I stopped there.'
How did you deploy the model, and how did you monitor it afterwards?

Describe the path: model file or pipeline, API or batch job, container, environments, who called it and how, latency targets, rollout and rollback, then monitoring of logs, alerts, drift and quality, and the retraining process. Say whether it was cloud or on-premise and why. If you did not do deployment yourself, say what you handed over and what you learned from the engineers who did.
Also covers: cloud vs on-premise, monitoring, SLA, retraining.

'We shipped the model as a containerised REST service on the client's cloud, with a daily batch job as fallback. Alerts fired on error rate and on drift in three key features, and a monthly retrain was scheduled with a quality gate.'
Describe the environment you worked in, such as cluster size and Dev, UAT and Prod setups.

Give a straight description: where data lived (warehouse, data lake, Hadoop or Spark cluster, cloud storage), how big the compute was, how many nodes or instances per environment, how code moved from dev to UAT to prod, and what you personally configured versus used. The study notes describe a Cloudera CDH 5.8 cluster with 15 production servers; that is an old distribution, so describe your own real setup and do not invent one.

'Development ran on a shared GPU server, training on a cloud GPU instance, and production on three container replicas behind a load balancer. Spark jobs for feature building ran on a 10-node cluster.'
How would you rate yourself in machine learning, big data or deep learning?

Be honest and anchored to evidence. A number alone means little; say what you can do at that level and what you are still learning. Avoid 10 out of 10. A good frame is: 'I'm strong at X (with an example), comfortable with Y, and currently learning Z.' It shows self-awareness, which interviewers value more than a high number.
Also covers: self-assessment, strengths, growth areas.

'About a 7 in classical ML: I've shipped three models end to end and can explain the maths behind them. In deep learning I'm about 5: I've fine-tuned vision and text models but haven't trained large ones from scratch.'
Which algorithms and areas have you explored, and what is your specialisation?

Name the algorithms you can genuinely discuss in depth, grouped by family (linear models, trees and boosting, clustering, dimensionality reduction, text and vision models), and then your focus area with a project that proves it. A long list you cannot defend backfires; interviewers will pick any item and probe. If you are broad, say 'I'm a generalist, let's talk about your specific need.'
'Mostly tabular modelling: regularised regression, random forests, XGBoost, plus k-means and PCA for segmentation. I have lighter experience with CNNs for images and TF-IDF text classifiers.'
How do you answer 'what are your expectations, future objectives, and why are you leaving?'

Keep it positive, specific and truthful. Expectations: work on real problems with data and people who can teach you, and clear ownership. Objectives: grow in a direction that matches the role (for example deeper in deployment or experimentation). Leaving: focus on what you want to learn or do next, not on blaming your employer, and connect it to this company's work. Do your research on the company so the answer sounds like it belongs to them.
Also covers: motivation, career story.
'I've enjoyed building models, and I now want to own more of the path to production. Your team ships models used by millions, so I'd learn deployment and monitoring at scale.'
How many projects have you worked on, and which were most relevant?

Give a short count and categories, then pick the two most relevant to this role and give a one-line result for each. Honesty about scale matters: say whether projects were production work, proofs of concept or personal projects.

'Five projects in three years: two in production (churn and demand forecasting), two proofs of concept (document classification and image defect detection) and one competition entry. The churn model is most relevant to your role.'
Given a new business problem, how do you approach it end to end?

I would restate the problem and the decision it supports, define the success metric and a baseline to beat, and ask what data exists and whether it is allowed to be used. Then explore and clean data, build a simple model, evaluate with the right metric and validation, iterate on features and models, check fairness and robustness, and plan deployment, monitoring and retraining before building. I would also ask whether machine learning is needed at all, because rules or analytics can be enough.
Also covers: problem framing, baseline, metric choice, deployment plan.

'Reduce late deliveries.' I would clarify whether the aim is predicting lateness or reducing it, define the metric (late rate, cost), start with a rule-based baseline, and only then build a model, with a plan for how dispatchers will use the prediction.
How do you explain a model's result to a non-technical stakeholder?

Start with the decision and the outcome in business terms, not the algorithm: what the model does, how good it is (use a number they care about, like 'catches 8 of 10 fraud cases with 1 false alarm per 20'), when it fails, and what you recommend. Use an analogy or a concrete example, a simple chart, and feature explanations (SHAP summary or top drivers) rather than equations. State uncertainty and the next step.
Also covers: storytelling, uncertainty, trade-offs.
Instead of 'AUC is 0.87', say: 'If we call the 500 highest-risk customers each week, about 200 of them would have left; without the model we'd reach about 75.'
Your model works in the notebook but performs badly in production. What do you check?

I would check, in order: data differences (training-serving skew, different preprocessing, missing or late features), leakage that inflated the offline score, a train-test split that did not mimic production, drift between the training period and now, label delay or definition mismatches, bugs in the serving code, and a threshold that was tuned on the wrong data. I'd replay logged production inputs through the offline pipeline and compare outputs row by row to find where they diverge.
Also covers: skew, leakage, drift, shadow mode.
Offline AUC 0.91, live 0.74. Replaying logged requests shows 'days since signup' was computed in UTC offline and local time online, shifting a key feature for a fifth of users.
Tell me about a time a project failed or a model underperformed.

Pick a real, modest failure and tell it with ownership: what the goal was, what went wrong (a flawed assumption, bad data, a misunderstood requirement), how you found out, what you did, and what changed in your process afterwards. Interviewers look for honesty, learning and a calm response, not for a hidden success story.

'Our recommender looked great offline but did not move clicks. The offline test used items users had already seen. We redesigned evaluation with a time-based split and an online A/B test, and I now insist on both before any launch.'
What are empirical risk minimisation (ERM) and PAC learning?

ERM is the principle behind most supervised learning: since you cannot compute the true error over all possible data, you choose the model that minimises the average loss on your training sample, and hope it generalises. Statistical learning theory studies when that hope is justified; regularisation and model complexity limits control the gap between training error and true error. PAC (probably approximately correct) learning formalises it: a class of functions is PAC-learnable if, with enough samples, an algorithm finds with high probability (1 - delta) a hypothesis whose error is below a small epsilon. It is theory-heavy and mostly asked in research-oriented interviews.
Also covers: empirical vs true risk, generalisation, sample complexity.

If you train a spam filter on 10,000 emails, ERM picks the filter with the lowest error on those emails; learning theory tells you how many emails you would need before that error is likely close to the error on future mail.
What are SENet, FPN, SPPNet, Highway Networks and similar architecture ideas?

These are building blocks introduced in influential papers. SENet's squeeze-and-excitation blocks reweight channels (a form of channel attention) at tiny cost. Feature Pyramid Networks combine feature maps at several scales so detectors find both small and large objects. SPPNet's spatial pyramid pooling produces a fixed-length vector from any image size. Highway Networks used learned gates on skip connections, a precursor of ResNet's identity shortcuts. ZFNet tuned AlexNet by visualising its layers, and FractalNet is a deep, shortcut-free alternative design. You rarely need details; know the idea in one sentence.
A detection model that struggles with small objects often adds an FPN, which lets high-resolution features feed the detector head, so small items are not lost after pooling.
What are neural architecture search (NAS) and DetNAS?

Neural architecture search automates the design of network architectures, using methods such as reinforcement learning, evolutionary search or gradient-based relaxations to explore a space of building blocks and pick those that score best on validation data. It can discover efficient models such as the EfficientNet family (together with compound scaling), but early versions needed enormous compute. DetNAS applies the same idea to object-detection backbones. For most teams, picking and fine-tuning a proven architecture is more practical.
Instead of hand-picking a mobile-friendly network, NAS searches thousands of candidate cell designs for the best accuracy under a latency limit on a target phone.
What is CenterNet, and what is anchor-free detection?

Anchor-based detectors place many predefined boxes and refine them, which needs hand-tuned sizes and many candidates. Anchor-free detectors predict object locations directly. Note that two different papers are both called CenterNet: one detects each object as a centre point and regresses its size, the other (keypoint triplets) detects corners and a centre keypoint to verify boxes. Check which one an interviewer means.
A detector that outputs a heat map where peaks mark object centres, plus width and height values, avoids anchor tuning and non-maximum suppression in many cases.
What are Task2Vec, meta-learning and multi-task learning?

Multi-task learning trains one model on several related tasks at once so they share representations. Meta-learning trains across many tasks so adaptation to a new one is fast. Task2Vec, as I understand the paper, represents a whole task as a fixed-length vector so tasks can be compared and the best pre-trained model for a new task can be selected; verify the details in the paper before quoting it. All three share the aim of reusing knowledge across tasks.
Before fine-tuning, a team wants to know which of 10 pre-trained models is closest to its new task; a task-embedding method gives a ranking without fine-tuning every candidate.
What research ideas should I know in NLP from 2018 to 2020 beyond BERT?

Several specialised ideas appear in the study notes: decaNLP trained one model to do ten NLP tasks framed as question answering; Universal Transformers add recurrence over depth to transformers; StarSpace learns embeddings for many kinds of objects in one space; TransferTransfo fine-tunes a pre-trained transformer for chat; Wizard of Wikipedia is a dataset for knowledge-grounded dialogue; ERASER benchmarks whether models give faithful rationales; Event2Mind and SWAG are commonsense-reasoning tasks, and pair2vec learns word-pair representations. They are mostly of historical or specialised interest now, since large language models absorbed many of these aims.
Also covers: commonsense inference, benchmarks, dialogue systems.

If an interviewer asks about SWAG, say it is a multiple-choice benchmark of what happens next in a grounded situation, built with adversarial filtering to reduce shortcuts, and that later pre-trained models solved it largely.
What is a Boltzmann machine, and what is a restricted Boltzmann machine?

A Boltzmann machine is an energy-based probabilistic network of stochastic binary units that learns a distribution over its inputs; training it fully is slow. A restricted Boltzmann machine removes connections within a layer (visible units connect only to hidden units), which makes training practical with contrastive divergence. RBMs were used in early deep-belief networks, collaborative filtering and feature learning (Hinton's group pioneered them), and have largely been replaced by autoencoders, GANs and transformers.
In a 2000s-era recommender, an RBM learns hidden 'taste' units from users' ratings, but today the same job is done by matrix factorisation or two-tower networks.
How do you handle an interview question about a paper or method you have not heard of?

Say so honestly, then show how you would reason: ask what problem it addresses, think about which family it belongs to (architecture, loss, data or training technique), and relate it to something you know. Offer to explain the closest idea you do know. Never bluff names, numbers or results; interviewers can tell, and trust is the thing at stake.
Also covers: honesty, reasoning from first principles.
'I haven't read about that exact method. From the name it sounds like a variant of attention for images. If it works like squeeze-and-excitation, it reweights channels; is that close?'
How do you keep up with research and judge whether a new method is worth using?

I follow a few trusted sources (conference proceedings, a small number of newsletters and blogs, and reproducible code), skim abstracts, and read the method and results sections of the few that matter. To judge a method: is the comparison fair, are gains larger than random-seed noise, does it work on data like mine, what are the compute and maintenance costs, and is there open code? Then test it on my own validation data against a strong baseline before adopting it.
A new boosting variant claims 1% gains on benchmarks. You run it against your tuned XGBoost on your dataset with repeated cross-validation; if the gain is within noise, you skip it.

Training an existing model a little more on your own examples so it adopts a style or skill. Slower and costlier than changing the prompt.
A cheap way to fine-tune by training only a small add-on instead of the whole model.

Shrinking a model by storing its numbers with less precision, so it runs faster and cheaper with a small quality loss.
A model that handles more than text, for example images, audio or video.

One of the most capable, newest models from the top labs. Usually the most expensive.

Putting a few worked examples in the prompt so the model copies the pattern.

Something that used to work breaking after a change. Regression tests catch this before users do.

Quality slowly decaying because the world, the data or the users change after launch.
How long a user waits for a response. Lower is faster.

The wait time that 99 out of 100 requests beat. It shows the slowest, rare cases.
How much work the system completes per second or minute.

Showing the reply word by word as it is produced, instead of waiting for the whole answer.
Saving a result so the next identical request is answered instantly and cheaply.

Handling more load by adding more machines, rather than buying one bigger machine.

Copies of data may briefly disagree but will match shortly. Fine for like counts; risky for bank balances.
A way to spread data over servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small part of it.
One item that gets a huge share of traffic, like a celebrity profile, overloading the machine that holds it.

Turns a list of raw scores into probabilities that add to 1. Used for multi-class outputs.
When the learning signal shrinks to almost nothing as it travels back through many layers, so early layers barely learn.
Rescaling a layer's inputs to a steady range during training, which makes training faster and more stable.
Starting from a model already trained on a large dataset and adapting it to your smaller task, instead of training from scratch.
Convolutional neural network: a network that slides small filters across an image to detect edges, shapes and objects. The standard for images.
Recurrent neural network: a network that reads a sequence step by step and keeps a memory of what came before.
A type of RNN with gates that decide what to remember and forget, so it handles longer sequences than a plain RNN.
A simpler cousin of the LSTM with fewer gates. Often just as good and faster to train.
A network that squeezes its input into a small code and then rebuilds it. Used for compression, denoising and spotting anomalies.
Generative adversarial network: two networks compete, one making fake samples and one trying to spot them, until the fakes look real.
A measure of how mixed or unpredictable a set of labels is. Zero means all the same class; higher means more mixed.
Another measure of how mixed a group is. Decision trees pick splits that lower it the most.
How much a split reduces entropy, in other words how much cleaner the groups become after splitting.
Training many models on random resamples of the data and averaging them, which lowers variance. Random forest is bagging with trees.
Building models one after another, each one focusing on the mistakes of the previous ones. Gradient boosting is the strong tabular-data default.
Many decision trees, each trained on a random sample of rows and features, voting together. Robust and hard to overfit.
Fast, widely used gradient-boosting libraries that often win on tabular data.
Support vector machine: finds the boundary that separates classes with the widest possible margin.
A shortcut that lets an SVM separate data that is not linearly separable by working as if the data were in a higher-dimensional space.
A fast classifier that applies Bayes' rule and assumes features are independent. Often a strong baseline for text.
K-nearest neighbours: predicts from the k most similar training examples. No training step, but slow on big data.
A clustering method that groups points around k centres, moving the centres until the groups settle.
Principal component analysis: squeezes many correlated features into fewer new ones that keep most of the variation.
A method for drawing high-dimensional data in 2D so similar items sit together. Great for pictures, not for modelling.
A faster alternative to t-SNE for visualising and reducing high-dimensional data.
When input features are strongly correlated with each other, which makes linear-model coefficients unstable and hard to interpret.
Variance inflation factor: a score for how much a feature is explained by the other features. High values (often above 5 or 10) signal multicollinearity.
When the size of a model's errors changes across the range of the data, for example bigger errors for bigger values.
Turning a category into separate 0/1 columns, one per value, so models can use it.
Putting numeric features on a similar range, which matters for distance-based and gradient-based models.
Creating new, more useful input columns from raw data, such as 'days since last purchase'.
A setting you choose before training (like learning rate or tree depth), as opposed to weights the model learns.
A table of correct and wrong predictions: true and false positives and negatives.
How likely you would see a result at least this extreme if there were really no effect. Small values suggest the effect is not just chance. It is not the probability the hypothesis is true.
The default assumption of 'no effect' that a statistical test tries to find evidence against.
Wrongly concluding there is an effect when there is not (a false alarm).
Missing a real effect (a missed detection).
A range of plausible values for a quantity, built so that, over many repeats, a stated share (such as 95%) of such ranges would contain the true value.
The average of many independent samples tends to follow a bell-shaped (normal) curve, whatever the original data looks like.
The symmetric bell-shaped distribution, described by its mean and standard deviation.
A time series whose average, spread and patterns do not change over time. Many forecasting models need it.
A classic forecasting model that combines past values (AR), differencing to remove trend (I) and past errors (MA).
Plots showing how strongly a time series correlates with its own past values, used to choose ARIMA settings.
A statistical test for whether a time series is stationary.
A score that rates a word as important in a document if it appears often there but rarely across other documents.
A method that learns word vectors so words used in similar contexts end up close together.
A transformer model from Google that reads text in both directions. Widely used as a pre-trained base for classification and search.
How surprised a language model is by real text. Lower is better.
Named entity recognition: finding and labelling names of people, places, organisations and similar items in text.
Crudely chopping word endings to a common root (running becomes run).
Reducing a word to its proper dictionary form using grammar (better becomes good).
Intersection over union: how much a predicted box overlaps the true box, from 0 to 1. Used to judge object detection.
Non-maximum suppression: after detection, keeping the best box and removing overlapping duplicates.
Mean average precision: the standard score for object detectors, averaging precision across classes and thresholds.
A chain of steps (clean, scale, model) bundled so the same steps run identically in training and prediction.
Recommending items by finding users with similar tastes and suggesting what they liked.
Finding items that are often bought together, such as 'people who buy bread often buy butter'.
Spotting rare data points that do not fit the usual pattern, such as fraud or equipment faults.
A rule for updating a belief with new evidence: posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence.
Choosing the model parameters that make the data you saw most probable.
Like maximum likelihood but also weighs a prior belief about the parameters.
The chance a test detects a real effect of a given size. Higher with more data and bigger effects.
Ways to tighten the significance threshold when you run many tests, so chance findings do not slip through.
Estimating uncertainty by resampling your own data with replacement many times.
A direction a matrix only stretches, never turns; the eigenvalue is how much. Behind PCA.
Singular value decomposition: splits a matrix into rotations and scalings. Used for compression, recommenders and PCA.
A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another. Cross-entropy loss is closely related.
How much knowing one variable tells you about another, including non-linear links.
A hidden factor that affects both the cause and the outcome and fakes a link between them.
When a trend in every subgroup reverses after the groups are combined.
A way to make A/B tests more sensitive by using each user's pre-test behaviour to cancel noise.
Comparing the before/after change of a treated group with that of a similar untreated group.
Predicting who is actually persuaded by an action, not just who will buy.
A small penalty on large weights during training, equivalent to L2 regularization in plain SGD.
Popular training optimisers that adapt the step size for each weight and smooth the updates. AdamW is the usual choice for transformers.
Rescaling a layer's values for each example separately. Standard in transformers.
A shortcut that adds a layer's input to its output, helping very deep networks train.
Capping the size of gradients so one huge update cannot wreck training.
Smooth activation functions used in modern transformers instead of plain ReLU.
Whether predicted probabilities match reality: of things called 80% likely, about 80% should happen.
Doing most maths in 16-bit numbers to train faster and use less memory.
Extra information added so a transformer knows the order of words.
Rotary position embeddings: a way of encoding word position that many recent language models use.
Running several attention operations in parallel so the model can track different relationships at once.
A rule that stops a token from seeing later tokens, so a model learns to predict the next word fairly.
A faster, memory-saving way to compute exact attention.
Sharing keys and values between attention heads to shrink the cache and speed up serving.
A model made of many small expert blocks where a router uses only a few per token, giving big capacity at lower compute.
Common ways to split text into sub-word tokens by merging frequent pieces.
Findings that model quality improves predictably with more parameters, data and compute; Chinchilla showed many models were under-trained.
A transformer that treats an image as a sequence of patches.
A model trained to put images and their captions close together, so it can classify images from text labels.
An image generator that starts from noise and removes it step by step, guided by a text prompt.
A sequence model with a compact running state, linear in length. Mamba is a well-known example.
